WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Modern era
======================================================================

{{Short description|Current period of history}}
{{Redirect|Modern age}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2026}}
{{Use American English|date=October 2026}}

{{Human history}}

The '''modern era''', or the '''modern period''', is considered the current [[historical period]] of [[human history]]. It was originally applied to the [[history of Europe]] and [[Western history]] for events that came after [[classical antiquity]] and the [[Middle Ages]], often from around the year 1500. An example is the [[Reformation]], which gave rise to [[Protestantism]] in [[History of Germany|Germany]] and elsewhere. Since the 1990s, it has been more common among historians to refer to the period after the Middle Ages and up to the 19th century as the [[early modern period]]. The modern period is today more often used for events from the 19th century until today. The time from the end of [[World War II]] (1945) can also be described as being part of [[contemporary history]]. The common definition of the modern period today is often associated with events such as the [[French Revolution]], the [[Industrial Revolution]], and the transition from [[nationalism]] toward the [[liberal international order]].

The modern period has been a period of significant development in the fields of science, politics, warfare, and technology. It has also been an [[Age of Discovery]] and [[globalization]]. During this time, the [[European powers]] and later their colonies strengthened their political, economic, and cultural [[colonization]] of the rest of the world. It also created a new modern lifestyle and has permanently changed the way people around the world live.<ref>{{Cite web |date=6 October 2023 |title=Colonialism facts and information |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/colonialism |access-date=1 August 2024 |website=Culture |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=How does colonialism shape the world we live in? |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/program/the-stream/2019/12/9/how-does-colonialism-shape-the-world-we-live-in |access-date=1 August 2024 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref> 

In the [[#19th century|19th]] and early [[#20th century|20th centuries]], [[modernism|modernist]] art, politics, science, and culture came to dominate not only Western Europe and North America, but almost every area on the globe, including [[Anti-Western sentiment|movements thought of as opposed to]] the Western world and globalization. The modern era is closely associated with the development of [[individualism]], [[capitalism]], [[socialism]], urbanization, and a belief in the positive possibilities of technological and political progress.

The [[Modern era#World War I|brutal]] [[Modern era#World War II|wars]] and [[Cold War|other conflicts of this era]], many of which come from the effects of rapid change, and the connected [[Detraditionalization|loss of strength of traditional religious]] and ethical norms, have led to many [[Modernism#Criticism of late modernity|reactions against modern development]]. [[Optimism]] and the [[Whig history|belief in constant progress]] have been most recently criticized by [[postmodernism]], while the [[Eurocentrism|dominance]] of Western Europe and North America over the rest of the world has been criticized by [[postcolonialism|postcolonial theory]].

==Terminology==
Eras cannot easily be defined for [[periodization]], the process of categorizing the past into quantified, named blocks of time for the purpose of analysis. 1500 is an approximate starting period for the modern era because many major events caused the Western world to change around then: from the [[fall of Constantinople]] (1453), [[Johannes Gutenberg|Gutenberg]]'s moveable-type [[printing press]] (1450s), and [[Christopher Columbus]]'s voyage to the Americas (1492), to the [[Reformation]] begun with [[Martin Luther]]'s [[Ninety-five Theses]] (1517).

The term "modern" was coined shortly before 1585 to describe the beginning of a new era.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia|title=modern|encyclopedia=The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language|publisher=Houghton Mifflin|year=2000|url=http://www.bartleby.com/61/28/M0362800.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080622132303/http://www.bartleby.com/61/28/M0362800.html|archive-date=22 June 2008|edition=4th|access-date=19 December 2022}}</ref> It was long thought that the term "early modern" was invented either in the 1930s, to distinguish the time between the Middle Ages and the late Enlightenment (1800),<ref>''New Dictionary of the History of Ideas'', Volume 5, Detroit 2005. s.v. "Modernism and Modern".</ref> or the mid-20th century, and only gained traction in the 1960s.{{sfn|Nipperdey|2022|p=199}} Justus Nipperdey pointed to its widespread usage by American historians around 1900 already, adding: 'In the interwar years the term permeated all areas of professional activity from textbooks and graduate school seminars to conferences, research articles, and job descriptions.'{{sfn|Nipperdey|2022|p=199}} The difference between "early modern" and "modern" was defined by the [[French Revolution]] and the [[Industrial Revolution]].{{sfn|Nipperdey|2022|p=199}} The European [[Renaissance]] (14th–16th centuries), which started in Italy, is an important transition period beginning in the [[Late Middle Ages]] and marking the change into early modern history.<ref name="History">[https://www.history.com/articles/renaissance Renaissance". ''History''. A&E Television Networks, LLC, 2018]</ref>

Sometimes distinct from the modern periods themselves, the terms "[[modernity]]" and "[[modernism]]" refer to a new way of thinking, distinct from previous ways of thinking such as medieval thinking. "[[Postmodernism]]", coined in 1949, describes a movement in art rather than a period of history, and is usually applied to the arts, but not to any events of recent history.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/postmodern|title=Definition of POSTMODERN|website=merriam-webster.com|date=2 June 2023|access-date=9 October 2022|archive-date=1 January 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080101091725/http://www.m-w.com/dictionary/postmodern|url-status=live}}</ref> This changed when [[postmodernity]] was coined to describe major changes in the 1960s in economy, society, culture, and philosophy.

These terms stem from European history. In worldwide usage, such as in China, India, and Islam, the terms are applied in a different way, but often in the context of their contact with European culture in the [[Age of Discovery]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nlm.nih.gov/exhibition/islamic_medical/islamic_14.html|title=Islamic Culture and the Medical Arts: Late Medieval and Early Modern Medicine|website=www.nlm.nih.gov|access-date=9 October 2022|archive-date=23 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180423084551/https://www.nlm.nih.gov/exhibition/islamic_medical/islamic_14.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Characteristics==
Changes, mostly seen as advances, in all areas of human activity—politics, [[Industry (economics)|industry]], society, economics, commerce, transport, communication, [[mechanization]], [[automation]], science, medicine, technology, religion, the arts, and other aspects of culture—appear to have transformed an ''Old World'' into the ''Modern'' or ''New World''. In each case, the identification of the change over time can be used to demarcate the old and old-fashioned from the modern.<ref>{{cite book |last=Giddens |first=Anthony |title=The Consequences of Modernity |year=1990 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=978-0-8047-1891-2 |pages=1–5}}</ref>

Starting in western countries, the modern world has seen a systematic re-evaluation of [[value system]]s, [[monarchy|monarchical]] regimes, and [[feudalism|feudal]] economic systems. These have often been replaced by democratic and liberal ideas in the areas of politics, science, psychology, sociology, and economics.<ref>{{cite book |last=Fukuyama |first=Francis |title=The Origins of Political Order: From Prehuman Times to the French Revolution |publisher=Farrar, Straus and Giroux |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-84668-256-8 |pages=321–323}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Habermas |first=Jürgen |title=The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere |year=1989 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-58108-0 |pages=73–75}}</ref>

Some events of modern history, though born out of contexts not entirely new, show a new way of perceiving the world. The concept of modernity interprets the general meaning of these events and seeks explanations for major developments.<ref>{{cite book |last=Berman |first=Marshall |title=All That Is Solid Melts into Air: The Experience of Modernity |year=1982 |publisher=Verso |isbn=978-0-14-010962-7 |pages=14–17}}</ref> Historians analyze the events taking place in Modern Times, since the so-called "[[Middle Ages]]" (between Modern and [[Ancient Times]]).<ref>{{cite book |last=Davis |first=Natalie Zemon |title=Society and Culture in Early Modern France |year=1975 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=978-0-8047-0972-9 |pages=3–5}}</ref>

==Early modern period==
{{Main|Early modern period|Renaissance|Early modern Europe}}

===Late 15th to 17th century===
{{Further|15th century|16th century|17th century}}
[[File:Printing towns incunabula.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|[[Global spread of the printing press|Spread of printing]] by [[Johannes Gutenberg]] from [[Mainz]] in Europe in the 15th century]]

====Renaissance and Reformation (c. 1400–1550)====
* [[Johannes Gutenberg]]'s movable‐type [[printing press]] (c. 1450s) ushered in the information age and rise of newspapers.<ref>{{cite book |last=Eisenstein |first=Elizabeth L. |title=The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2005}}</ref>
* Conquest of [[Constantinople]] by the [[Ottoman Empire]] (1453) marked the fall of the [[Byzantine Empire]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Runciman |first=Steven |title=The Fall of Constantinople, 1453 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1965}}</ref>
* [[Christopher Columbus]]'s first voyage to the Americas (1492) initiated sustained contact between Europe and the New World.<ref>{{cite book |last=Crosby |first=Alfred W. |title=The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492 |publisher=Praeger |year=1972}}</ref>
* [[Amerigo Vespucci]]'s [[New_World#Mundus_Novus|Mundus Novus]] letter (1503), the first explicit articulation in print of the hypothesis that the lands discovered by European navigators to the west were not the edges of Asia but rather an entirely different continent, is published.<ref>The Vespucci letter sent from Bezeguiche was not published, but was maintained in manuscript form and was published by F.A. de Varnhagen in 1865 ({{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=R9QOAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA78 |title=Amerígo Vespucci, son caractère, ses écrits ... sa vie et ses navigations ... |last=de Varnhagen |first=Francisco Adolfo |year=1865 |pages=78–82 |via=Google Books |language=fr}}).</ref>
* [[Niccolò Machiavelli]]'s ''[[The Prince]]'' (c. 1513), a foundational work of modern [[political philosophy]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Machiavelli |first=Niccolò |title=The Prince |translator-last=Mansfield |translator-first=Harvey C. |publisher=University of Chicago Press |year=1998 |isbn=978-0-226-50044-7}}</ref>
* [[Martin Luther]]'s posting of the [[95 Theses]] (1517) ignited the [[Reformation]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Bainton |first=Roland H. |title=Here I Stand: A Life of Martin Luther |publisher=Abingdon Press |year=1950}}</ref>
* The broader [[Age of Discovery]] saw unprecedented maritime exploration and early colonial empires.<ref>{{cite book |last=Buisseret |first=David |title=The Exploration of the New World, 1400–1600: Maps and Narratives |publisher=Routledge |year=1992}}</ref>
* [[Nicolaus Copernicus]]'s ''[[De revolutionibus orbium coelestium]]'' (1543) proposes that [[Copernican heliocentrism|the Earth revolves around the Sun]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Kuhn |first=Thomas S. |title=The Copernican Revolution |publisher=Harvard University Press |year=1957}}</ref>
* [[Council of Trent]] (1545) begins the Catholic [[Counter-Reformation]].<ref>{{cite book |last=O'Malley |first=John W. |title=Trent: What Happened at the Council |publisher=Belknap Press: An Imprint of Harvard University Press |year=2013 |isbn=978-0-674-06697-7 |location=Cambridge, MA}}</ref>
* Rise of [[Mercantilism]] as the prevailing economic theory.<ref>{{cite book |last=Heckscher |first=Eli F. |title=Mercantilism |publisher=Routledge |year=1994}}</ref>

[[File:Pleiades_Sidereus_Nuncius_(cropped).png|thumb|200px|Galileo reported in the ''[[Starry Messenger]]'' (1610) that he saw at least ten times more stars through the telescope than are visible to the naked eye.]]

====Scientific Revolution and early Baroque (c. 1550–1700)====
* [[Tycho Brahe]] observes a [[SN_1572#Historic_description|new star]] (1572), brighter than any star or planet, that ought not to exist.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wootton |first=David |author-link=David Wootton (historian) |title=The Invention of Science: A New History of the Scientific Revolution |publisher=Penguin |year=2015 |pages=12-13 |isbn=978-0-06-175952-9 |quote=On the evening of 11 November 1572, soon after sunset, a young Danish nobleman called Tycho Brahe was looking at the night sky. Almost directly above his head he noticed a star brighter than any other, a star that ought not to have been there.}}</ref>
* Defeat of the [[Spanish Armada]] (1588) secured English naval supremacy and enabled the rise of the [[British Empire]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Mattingly |first=Garrett |title=The Armada |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt |year=1959}}</ref>
* [[Johannes Kepler]]'s ''[[Astronomia nova]]'' (1609) includes the first mention of elliptical planetary orbits.<ref>{{Cite book | last=Voelkel | first=James R. | title=The composition of Kepler's Astronomia nova | date=2001 | publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] | location=Princeton  | isbn=0-691-00738-1 | pages=1}}</ref>
* [[Galileo Galilei]]'s ''[[Starry Messenger]]'' (1610) was the first published work of observations made through a telescope.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sharratt |first=M. |title=Galileo: Decisive Innovator |date=1994 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-56671-1 |location=Cambridge}}</ref>
* The [[Thirty Years' War]] (1618–1648) devastated Europe and reshaped its political order.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wilson |first=Peter H. |title=Europe's Tragedy: A New History of the Thirty Years' War |publisher=Penguin Press |year=2009}}</ref>
* The [[Peace of Westphalia]] treaties (1648) ended multiple European conflicts and established the principle of state sovereignty.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Croxton |first1=Derek |last2=Tischer |first2=Anuschka |title=The Peace of Westphalia: A Historical Dictionary |publisher=Greenwood Press |year=1999 |isbn=978-0-313-28073-3}}</ref>
* [[Isaac Newton]]'s ''[[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica]]'' (1687) formulates the [[Newton's laws of motion|laws of motion]] and the [[Newton's law of universal gravitation|law of universal gravitation]].<ref>{{cite book | last = Cohen | first = I. Bernard | title = Introduction to Newton's ''Principia'' | publisher = Harvard University Press | date = 1971 | location = Cambridge, Massachusetts | isbn = 978-0674461758 | lccn = 75151528 }}</ref> 
* The [[Glorious Revolution]] (1688) in England affirmed parliamentary supremacy over the monarchy.<ref>{{cite book |last=Vallance |first=Edward |title=The Glorious Revolution: 1688—Britain's Fight for Liberty |publisher=Little, Brown |year=2001}}</ref>
* Early reign of [[Louis XIV]] (1643–1715), epitomizing the [[Age of Absolutism]] in France.<ref>{{cite book |last=Mansel |first=Philip |title=Louis XIV |publisher=John Murray |year=2019}}</ref>

===18th century===
{{Main|18th century}}

==== Age of Enlightenment and Revolution (c. 1700–1800) ====
{{further|Age of Enlightenment}}
* [[War of the Spanish Succession]] (1701–1714), concluded by the [[Peace of Utrecht]] and redrawing dynastic and colonial boundaries.<ref>{{cite book |last=Browning |first=Reed |title=The War of the Spanish Succession |publisher=University of Pennsylvania Press |year=1993}}</ref>
* [[War of the Austrian Succession]] (1740–1748), contesting Habsburg succession and reshaping Central Europe.<ref>{{cite book |last=Duffy |first=Christopher |title=The Military Experience in the Age of Reason |publisher=Routledge |year=1987}}</ref>
* [[Seven Years' War]] (1756–1763), the first truly global conflict, spanning Europe, North America (known in the US as the [[French and Indian War]]), India and the Caribbean.<ref>{{cite book |last=Baugh |first=Daniel A. |title=The Global Seven Years War 1754–1763 |publisher=Pearson Education |year=2011}}</ref>
* Onset of the [[Industrial Revolution]] (c. 1760), beginning in Britain with mechanization of textile production and development of the steam engine.<ref>{{cite book |last=Mokyr |first=Joel |title=The Enlightened Economy: An Economic History of Britain 1700–1850 |publisher=Yale University Press |year=2009}}</ref>
* [[American Revolution]] (1775–1783), resulting in the independence of the United States of America.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wood |first=Gordon S. |title=The Radicalism of the American Revolution |publisher=Vintage Books |year=1993}}</ref>
* [[French Revolution]] (1789–1799), which overthrew the [[Bourbon monarchy]] and established the First [[French Republic]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Doyle |first=William |title=The Oxford History of the French Revolution |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1989}}</ref>
* [[Ottoman Old Regime]] (1703–1789) followed by the [[decline and modernization of the Ottoman Empire]].

==19th century==
{{Main|19th century}}

Historians sometimes define a nineteenth-century [[List of time periods|historical era]] from 1815 (the [[Congress of Vienna]]) to 1914 (the outbreak of [[World War I]]).<ref>{{cite book |last=Hobsbawm |first=Eric |title=The Age of Revolution: Europe 1789–1848 |publisher=Weidenfeld & Nicolson |year=1962}}</ref> Alternatively, Eric Hobsbawm defined the "[[long nineteenth century]]" as spanning from 1789 (the French Revolution) to 1914.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hobsbawm |first=Eric |title=The Age of Empire: 1875–1914 |publisher=Weidenfeld & Nicolson |year=1987}}</ref>

During this century, the Spanish, Portuguese, and Ottoman Empires began to decline. The Ottoman Empire suffered territorial losses in the eastern Mediterranean and Balkans.<ref>{{cite book |last=Quataert |first=Donald |title=The Ottoman Empire, 1700–1922 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2005}}</ref> The Holy Roman Empire was dissolved in 1806 by Emperor Francis II.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wilson |first=Peter H. |title=Heart of Europe: A History of the Holy Roman Empire |publisher=Belknap Press |year=2016}}</ref> The Mughal Empire effectively ended after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.<ref>{{cite book |last=Richards |first=John F. |title=The Mughal Empire |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1993}}</ref>

===Napoleonic era (1799–1815)===
{{Main|Napoleonic era}}

The Napoleonic era, regarded as the fourth phase of the [[French Revolution]], began with Napoleon's coup in 1799 and ended with his defeat at the [[Battle of Waterloo]] in 1815.<ref>{{cite book |last=Roberts |first=Andrew |title=Napoleon: A Life |publisher=Penguin |year=2014}}</ref> The subsequent [[Congress of Vienna]] (1814–1815) sought to restore the pre-Revolutionary balance of power across Europe.<ref>{{cite book |last=Jarrett |first=Mark |title=The Congress of Vienna and Its Legacy |publisher=I.B. Tauris |year=2013}}</ref>

=== Spreading of the Industrial Revolution ===
{{Main|Industrial Revolution}}
[[File:Maquina vapor Watt ETSIIM.jpg|thumb|211px|A Watt steam engine in [[Madrid]]. The development of the [[steam engine]] started the Industrial Revolution in England. The steam engine was created to pump water from coal mines, enabling them to be deepened beyond [[groundwater]] levels.]]

The Industrial Revolution was the major [[Technology|technological]], [[Socioeconomics|socioeconomic]], and [[Culture|cultural]] change in the late 18th and early 19th centuries that began in [[Kingdom of Great Britain|Britain]] and spread throughout the world. During that time, an [[Economic system|economy]] based on [[manual labour]] was replaced by one dominated by industry and the manufacture of machinery. It began with the mechanisation of the textile industries and the development of iron-making techniques, and trade expansion was enabled by the introduction of [[canal]]s, improved roads, and then railways. The introduction of [[Steam engine|steam power]] (fuelled primarily by coal) and powered machinery (mainly in [[textile manufacturing]]) underpinned the dramatic increases in production capacity.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Meier|first1=Gerald M.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CX9kBaVx4JkC&pg=PA98|title=Leading Issues in Economic Development|last2=Rauch|first2=James E.|date=2000|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-511589-5|page=98|access-date=8 February 2023|archive-date=31 March 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230331130624/https://books.google.com/books?id=CX9kBaVx4JkC&pg=PA98|url-status=live}}</ref> The development of all-metal [[machine tool]]s in the first two decades of the 19th century facilitated the manufacture of more production machines for manufacturing in other industries.

The date of the Industrial Revolution is not exact. [[Eric Hobsbawm]] held that it "broke out" in the 1780s and was not fully felt until the 1830s or 1840s,<ref>Eric Hobsbawm, ''The Age of Revolution: Europe 1789–1848'', Weidenfeld and Nicolson Ltd. {{ISBN|0-349-10484-0}}</ref> while [[T. S. Ashton]] held that it occurred roughly between 1760 and 1830 (in effect the reigns of [[George III]], the [[Regency era|Regency]], and [[George IV]]).<ref>{{cite book | author= Joseph E. Inikori| title= Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England: A Study in International Trade and Economic Development | page= 102 | publisher= Cambridge University Press|isbn= 0-521-01079-9}}</ref>

The effects spread throughout Western Europe and North America during the 19th century, eventually affecting the majority of the world. The impact of this change on society was enormous and is often compared to the [[Neolithic Revolution]], when mankind developed agriculture and gave up its [[nomad]]ic lifestyle.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Brown|first=Lester Russell|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5aCyfUsHM6kC&pg=PA93|title=Eco-economy: Building an Economy for the Earth|date=2003|publisher=Earthscan|isbn=978-1-85383-904-7|page=93|access-date=8 February 2023|archive-date=14 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230414231536/https://books.google.com/books?id=5aCyfUsHM6kC&pg=PA93|url-status=live}}</ref>

The First Industrial Revolution gave way to the [[Second Industrial Revolution]] around 1850, when technological and economic progress gained momentum with the development of steam-powered ships and railways, and later in the nineteenth century with the [[internal combustion engine]] and [[electric power]] generation.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

=== Decline and modernization of the Ottoman Empire ===
{{Main|Decline and modernization of the Ottoman Empire|History of the Ottoman Empire #Decline and modernization (1828–1908)}}

=== Late 19th century ===
Following the [[Napoleonic Wars]], the [[British Empire]] became the world's leading power, controlling one-quarter of the world's population and one-third of the land area.<ref>{{cite book |last=Ferguson |first=Niall |title=Empire: How Britain Made the Modern World |year=2004 |publisher=Penguin |isbn=978-0-14-100754-0 |pages=70–72}}</ref> It enforced a [[Pax Britannica]], encouraged trade, and battled rampant piracy.<ref>{{cite book |last=Marshall |first=P. J. |title=The Cambridge Illustrated History of the British Empire |year=2001 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-00254-7 |pages=142–145}}</ref>

[[Slavery]] was greatly reduced around the world. Following a successful [[Haitian Revolution|slave revolt in Haiti]], Britain forced the [[Barbary pirates]] to halt their practice of kidnapping and enslaving Europeans, passed the [[Slavery Abolition Act 1833]]—which banned slavery throughout its domain—and charged its navy with ending the global slave trade.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hochschild |first=Adam |title=Bury the Chains: Prophets and Rebels in the Fight to Free an Empire's Slaves |year=2005 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt |isbn=978-0-618-61907-8 |pages=331–335}}</ref> Slavery was then abolished in [[Emancipation reform of 1861 in Russia|Russia]] in 1861,<ref>{{cite book |last=Riasanovsky |first=Nicholas |title=A History of Russia |year=2005 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-515394-1 |pages=352–355}}</ref> by the [[Emancipation Proclamation]] in the United States in 1863,<ref>{{cite book |last=McPherson |first=James |title=Battle Cry of Freedom: The Civil War Era |year=1988 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-503863-7 |pages=557–560}}</ref> and in [[Lei Áurea|Brazil]] in 1888.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bethell |first=Leslie |title=The Abolition of the Brazilian Slave Trade: Britain, Brazil and the Slave Trade Question |year=1970 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-07459-9 |pages=412–415}}</ref> (see [[Abolitionism]]).

Following the abolition of the [[History of slavery|slave trade]], and propelled by economic exploitation, the [[Scramble for Africa]] was initiated formally at the [[Berlin West Africa Conference]] in 1884–1885.<ref>{{cite book |last=Pakenham |first=Thomas |title=The Scramble for Africa |publisher=Harper Collins |year=1991 |isbn=978-0-349-10449-2 |pages=112–115}}</ref> All the major European powers laid claim to the areas of Africa where they could exhibit a sphere of influence over the area. These claims did not have to have any substantial land holdings or treaties to be legitimate.<ref>{{cite book |last=Chamberlain |first=M.E. |title=The Scramble for Africa |publisher=Routledge |year=2010 |isbn=978-1-4082-2014-6 |pages=54–57}}</ref> The [[French Third Republic|French]] gained major ground in West Africa, the [[Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland|British]] in East Africa, and the [[History of Portugal (1834–1910)|Portuguese]] and [[Restoration (Spain)|Spanish]] at various points throughout the continent, while [[Leopold II of Belgium]] was able to retain his personal fiefdom, [[Belgian Congo|Congo]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Hochschild |first=Adam |title=King Leopold's Ghost: A Story of Greed, Terror, and Heroism in Colonial Africa |year=1998 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin |isbn=978-0-618-00190-3 |pages=88–92}}</ref>

Electricity, steel, and petroleum fuelled a [[Second Industrial Revolution]] which enabled [[German Empire|Germany]], [[Empire of Japan|Japan]], and the United States to become [[great power]]s that [[New Imperialism|raced to create empires of their own]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Mokyr |first=Joel |title=The Lever of Riches: Technological Creativity and Economic Progress |year=1990 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-507477-2 |pages=178–181}}</ref> However, [[Russian Empire|Russia]] and [[Qing dynasty|China]] failed to keep pace with the other world powers, which led to massive social unrest in both empires.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hobsbawm |first=Eric |title=The Age of Empire: 1875–1914 |year=1987 |publisher=Weidenfeld & Nicolson |isbn=978-0-297-79367-0 |pages=134–136}}</ref>

== 20th century ==
{{Main|20th century}}

While earlier centuries also saw significant developments, the ''20th century'' was distinguished by the unprecedented pace and global scale of economic, technological, and cultural changes.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hobsbawm |first=Eric |title=The Age of Extremes: The Short Twentieth Century, 1914–1991 |year=1994 |publisher=Michael Joseph |isbn=978-0-679-73005-7 |pages=7–9}}</ref>

Still, advancing technology and medicine have had a great impact even in the [[Global South]]. Large-scale industry and more centralized media made brutal dictatorships possible on an unprecedented scale in the middle of the century, leading to wars that were also unprecedented.<ref>{{cite book |last=Overy |first=Richard |title=The Dictators: Hitler's Germany, Stalin's Russia |publisher=Allen Lane |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-14-028149-1 |pages=16–20}}</ref> However, the increased communications contributed to [[democratization]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Diamond |first=Larry |title=The Spirit of Democracy: The Struggle to Build Free Societies Throughout the World |year=2008 |publisher=Times Books |isbn=978-0-8050-8913-4 |pages=56–58}}</ref>

Technological developments included the development of airplanes and [[space exploration]], [[nuclear technology]], advancement in [[genetics]], and the dawning of the [[Information Age]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Standage |first=Tom |title=The Victorian Internet |year=1998 |publisher=Walker & Company |isbn=978-0-8027-1366-7 |pages=100–102}}</ref>

Major political developments included the [[Israeli–Palestinian conflict]],<ref>{{cite book |last=Shlaim |first=Avi |title=The Iron Wall: Israel and the Arab World |year=2000 |publisher=Penguin Books |isbn=978-0-14-028870-4 |pages=4–7}}</ref> two world wars,<ref>{{cite book |last=Keegan |first=John |title=The First World War |publisher=Knopf |year=1998 |isbn=978-0-375-40052-0 |pages=14–17}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Beevor |first=Antony |title=The Second World War |year=2012 |publisher=Weidenfeld & Nicolson |isbn=978-0-297-86070-9 |pages=45–48}}</ref> and the [[Cold War]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Gaddis |first=John Lewis |title=The Cold War: A New History |year=2005 |publisher=Penguin Press |isbn=978-1-59420-062-5 |pages=21–25}}</ref> It also saw the former British Empire lose most of its remaining political power over Commonwealth countries, most notably by the division of the British crown into several sovereignties by the [[Statute of Westminster 1931|Statute of Westminster]],<ref>{{cite book |last=Townshend |first=Charles |title=The British Empire: A Very Short Introduction |year=2011 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-960541-5 |pages=106–107}}</ref> the [[patriation]] of constitutions by the [[Canada Act 1982]],<ref>{{cite book |last=Russell |first=Peter H. |title=Constitutional Odyssey: Can Canadians Become a Sovereign People? |year=2004 |publisher=University of Toronto Press |isbn=978-0-8020-8591-7 |pages=123–126}}</ref> and the [[Australia Act 1986]],<ref>{{cite book |last=Saunders |first=Cheryl |author-link=
Cheryl Saunders  |title=The Constitution of Australia: A Contextual Analysis |year=2011 |publisher=Hart Publishing |isbn=978-1-84113-734-6 |pages=68–70}}</ref> as well as the independence of countries such as India, [[Pakistan]], South Africa, and Ireland.<ref>{{cite book |last=Judt |first=Tony |title=Postwar: A History of Europe Since 1945 |year=2006 |publisher=Penguin Books |isbn=978-0-14-303775-0 |pages=91–93}}</ref>

=== World War I ===
{{Main|World War I}}

The First World War was a [[World war|world conflict]], lasting from July 1914 to the final [[Armistice with Germany (Compiègne)|Armistice]] on 11 November 1918. The [[Allies of World War I|Allied Powers]], led by the [[Britain in World War I|British Empire]], [[French Third Republic|France]], Russia until March 1918, Japan, and the United States after 1917, defeated the [[Central Powers]], led by the [[German Empire]], the [[Austro-Hungarian Empire]], and the [[Ottoman Empire]]. The war caused the disintegration of four empires—the Austro-Hungarian, German, Ottoman, and Russian ones—as well as radical change in the European and Middle Eastern maps. The Allied Powers before 1917 are sometimes referred to as the [[Triple Entente]], and the Central Powers are sometimes referred to as the [[Triple Alliance (1882)|Triple Alliance]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cartwright |first=Mark |date=2025-09-19 |title=The Pre-WWI Alliance System: Triple Entente v. Triple Alliance |url=https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2808/the-pre-wwi-alliance-system/ |journal=World History Encyclopedia |language=en}}</ref>

Much of the fighting in World War I took place along the [[Western Front (World War I)|Western Front]], within a system of opposing manned trenches and fortifications (separated by a "[[no man's land]]") running from the [[North Sea]] to the border of Switzerland. On the [[Eastern Front (World War I)|Eastern Front]], the vast eastern plains and limited rail network prevented a trench warfare stalemate from developing, although the scale of the conflict was just as large. Hostilities also occurred on and under the sea and—for the first time—from the air. More than 9 million soldiers died on the various battlefields, and nearly that many more in the participating countries' home fronts on account of food shortages and [[genocide]] committed under the cover of various civil wars and internal conflicts. Notably, more people died of the worldwide [[Spanish flu|influenza outbreak]] at the end of the war and shortly after than died in the hostilities. The unsanitary conditions engendered by the war, severe overcrowding in barracks, wartime propaganda interfering with public health warnings, and migration of so many soldiers around the world helped the outbreak become a [[pandemic]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Barry|first=John M.|author-link=John M. Barry|title=The Great Influenza: The Epic Story of the Greatest Plague in History|publisher=Viking Penguin|year=2004|isbn=0-670-89473-7|series=}}</ref>

Ultimately, World War I created a decisive break with the old [[New world order (politics)|world order]] that had emerged after the Napoleonic Wars, which was modified by the mid-19th century's nationalistic revolutions. The results of World War I would be important factors in the development of [[World War II]] approximately 20 years later.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

==== Dissolution of the Ottoman Empire ====
{{main| Middle Eastern theatre of World War I | Military of the Ottoman Empire | Dissolution of the Ottoman Empire | Occupied Enemy Territory Administration }}

=== Interwar period ===
{{Main|Interwar period}}

The Interwar period was the period between the end of World War I in 1918 and the beginning of World War II in 1939. It included the [[Roaring Twenties]], the [[Great Depression]], and the rise of [[communism]] in Russia and [[fascism]] in Italy and Germany.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

===World War II===
{{Main|World War II}}

World War II was a [[World war|global]] [[war|military conflict]] that took place in 1939–1945. It was the largest and deadliest war in history, culminating in [[the Holocaust]] and ending with the dropping of the [[atom bomb|atomic bomb]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Keegan |first=John |title=The Second World War |year=1989 |publisher=Penguin |isbn=978-0-14-011341-9 |pages=5–6}}</ref>

Although Japan had invaded China in 1937, the conventional view is that World War II began on 1 September 1939, when [[Nazi Germany]] invaded Poland. Within two days, the United Kingdom and France declared war on Germany, even though the fighting was confined to Poland. Pursuant to a then-secret provision of its non-aggression [[Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact]], the Soviet Union joined Germany on 17 September 1939 to conquer Poland and divide Eastern Europe.<ref>{{cite book |last=Roberts |first=Geoffrey |title=The Soviet Union and the Origins of the Second World War |year=1995 |publisher=Macmillan |isbn=978-0-333-64068-5 |pages=55–58}}</ref> The [[Allies of World War II|Allies]] were initially made up of Poland, the United Kingdom, France, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, as well as [[Commonwealth of Nations|British Commonwealth]] countries which were controlled directly by the UK, such as the [[British Raj|Indian Empire]]. All of these countries declared war on Germany in September 1939.<ref>{{cite book |last=Overy |first=Richard |title=Why the Allies Won |year=1995 |publisher=Pimlico |isbn=978-1-84595-065-1 |pages=3–4}}</ref>

Following the lull in fighting, known as the "[[Phoney War]]", Germany invaded western Europe in May 1940. Six weeks later, France, in the meantime attacked by Italy as well, surrendered to Germany, which then tried unsuccessfully to conquer Britain. On 27 September, Germany, Italy, and Japan signed a mutual defense agreement, the [[Tripartite Pact]], and were known as the [[Axis powers]]. Nine months later, on 22 June 1941, Germany launched a massive invasion of the Soviet Union, which prompted it to join the Allies. Germany was now engaged in fighting a war on two fronts.<ref>{{cite book |last=Beevor |first=Antony |title=The Second World War |year=2012 |publisher=Weidenfeld & Nicolson |isbn=978-0-297-84497-6 |pages=137–139}}</ref>

On 7 December 1941, [[Attack on Pearl Harbor|Japan attacked the United States at Pearl Harbor]], bringing it into the war on the side of the Allies. China also joined the Allies, as did most of the rest of the world. China was in turmoil at the time and attacked Japanese armies through guerrilla-type warfare. By the beginning of 1942, the alignment of the major combatants was as follows: the British Commonwealth, the Soviet Union, and the United States were fighting Germany and Italy; China, the British Commonwealth, and the United States were fighting Japan.<ref>{{cite book |last=Gilbert |first=Martin |title=The Second World War: A Complete History |year=1989 |publisher=Henry Holt |isbn=978-0-8050-0534-9|pages=223–225}}</ref> The United Kingdom, the United States, the Soviet Union, and China were referred to as a "trusteeship of the powerful" during World War II<ref name="Justus">{{cite book |last1=Doenecke |first1=Justus D. |last2=Stoler |first2=Mark A. |title=Debating Franklin D. Roosevelt's Foreign Policies, 1933–1945 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdMF9rX6mX8C&pg=PA62 |year=2005 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-0-8476-9416-7 |access-date=13 October 2019 |archive-date=3 December 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161203230343/https://books.google.com/books?id=xdMF9rX6mX8C&pg=PA62 |url-status=live |pages=62–63}}</ref> and were recognized as the Allied "Big Four" in the [[Declaration by United Nations]].<ref>Hoopes, Townsend, and Douglas Brinkley. ''FDR and the Creation of the U.N.'' (Yale University Press, 1997), pp. 155–160.</ref> These four countries were considered the "[[Four Policemen]]" or "Four Sheriffs" of the [[Allies of World War II|Allies]] and were the primary victors of World War II.<ref>{{cite book|first=John Lewis|last=Gaddis|title=The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941–1947|url=https://archive.org/details/unitedstatesorig0000gadd|url-access=registration|year=1972|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-12239-9|pages=[https://archive.org/details/unitedstatesorig0000gadd/page/24 24]–25}}</ref> Battles raged across all of Europe, in the North Atlantic Ocean, across North Africa, throughout Southeast Asia, throughout China, across the Pacific Ocean, and in the air over Japan. Italy surrendered in September 1943 and was split into a northern Germany-occupied [[puppet state]] and an Allies-friendly state in the south; Germany surrendered in May 1945. Following the [[atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]], [[surrender of Japan|Japan surrendered]], marking the end of the war on 2 September 1945.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hastings |first=Max |title=Inferno: The World at War, 1939–1945 |year=2011 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=978-0-307-27359-8 |pages=510–512}}</ref>

It is possible that around 62 million people [[World War II casualties|died in the war]]; estimates vary greatly. About 60% of all casualties were civilians, who died as a result of disease, starvation, [[genocide]] (in particular, the [[Holocaust]]), and aerial bombing.<ref>{{cite book |last=Ferguson |first=Niall |title=The War of the World: Twentieth-Century Conflict and the Descent of the West |year=2007 |publisher=Penguin |isbn=978-0-14-311239-6 |pages=413–416}}</ref> The former Soviet Union and China suffered the most casualties. Estimates place deaths in the Soviet Union at around 23 million, while China suffered about 10&nbsp;million. No country lost a greater portion of its population than Poland: approximately 5.6 million, or 16%, of its pre-war population of 34.8 million died.<ref>{{cite book |last=Snyder |first=Timothy |title=Bloodlands: Europe Between Hitler and Stalin |year=2012 |publisher=Basic Books |isbn=978-0-465-03297-6 |pages=67–69}}</ref> The Holocaust (which roughly means "burnt whole") was the deliberate and systematic murder of millions of Jews and other "unwanted" groups during World War II by the Nazi regime in Germany. Several differing views exist regarding whether it was intended to occur from the war's beginning or if the plans for it came about later. Regardless, persecution of Jews extended well before the war even started, such as during ''[[Kristallnacht]]'' (Night of Broken Glass). The Nazis used propaganda to great effect to stir up anti-Semitic feelings within ordinary Germans.<ref>{{cite book |last=Evans |first=Richard J. |title=The Third Reich at War |year=2008 |publisher=Penguin |isbn=978-1-59420-206-3 |pages=251–255}}</ref>

After World War II, Europe was informally split into Western and Soviet [[Sphere of influence|spheres of influence]]. Western Europe later aligned as [[NATO]], and Eastern Europe as the [[Warsaw Pact]]. There was a shift in power from Western Europe and the [[British Empire]] to the two new superpowers, the United States and the Soviet Union. These two rivals would later face off in the [[Cold War]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Leffler |first=Melvyn P. |title=A Preponderance of Power: National Security, the Truman Administration, and the Cold War |year=1993 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=978-0-8047-1924-7 |pages=15–17}}</ref> In Asia, the defeat of Japan led to its [[democratization]]. [[Chinese Civil War|China's civil war]] continued through and after the war, eventually resulting in the establishment of the People's Republic of China. The former colonies of the European powers began their road to independence.<ref>{{cite book |last=Darwin |first=John |title=After Tamerlane: The Rise and Fall of Global Empires, 1400–2000 |year=2008 |publisher=Bloomsbury Press |isbn=978-1-59691-393-6 |pages=357–360}}</ref>

=== Cold War ===
{{Main|Cold War}}{{See also|Contemporary history|Cold War in Asia}}{{History of the Cold War}}

The [[Cold War]] between the "West" (the United States, Western Europe, and Japan) and the "East" (the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe, and China) dominated politics from the end of World War II in 1945 until the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|collapse of the Soviet Union]] in 1991, at which point the Cold War ended and the [[post–Cold War era]] began (which includes most of the 1990s).<ref>{{cite book |last=Gaddis |first=John Lewis |title=The Cold War: A New History |year=2005 |publisher=Penguin Press |isbn=978-1-59420-062-5 |pages=35–40}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Leffler |first=Melvyn P. |title=For the Soul of Mankind: The United States, the Soviet Union, and the Cold War |year=2007 |publisher=Hill and Wang |isbn=978-0-374-53142-3|pages=80–85}}</ref>

The [[Korean War]], [[Vietnam War]], [[Soviet–Afghan War]], and [[Gulf War]] impacted political life, while the [[counterculture of the 1960s]] and the [[Information Age|rise of computers]] changed society in different, complex ways, including higher social and local mobility.<ref>{{cite book |last=Westad |first=Odd Arne |title=The Global Cold War: Third World Interventions and the Making of Our Times |year=2007 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-70314-7 |pages=212–217}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Castells |first=Manuel |title=The Rise of the Network Society |year=1996 |publisher=Blackwell Publishers |isbn=978-1-55786-617-2 |pages=3–8}}</ref>

== Post–Cold War era ==
{{See also|Contemporary history|End of history}}{{main|Post–Cold War era|21st century}}

=== 1990s ===
{{Main|1990s|Cold War (1985–1991)}}

At the end of the twentieth century, the world was at a major crossroads. Throughout the century, more technological advances had been made than in all of preceding history. Computers, the Internet, and other technologies radically altered daily lives.<ref>{{cite book |last=Standage |first=Tom |title=The Victorian Internet: The Remarkable Story of the Telegraph and the Nineteenth Century's On-line Pioneers |year=1998 |publisher=Walker & Company |isbn=978-0-8027-1342-1 |pages=200–202}}</ref> However, several problems faced the world during the Cold War period and the 1990s that followed.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

First of all, the gap between rich and poor nations continued to widen. Some said that this problem could not be fixed, arguing that there was a set amount of wealth and it could only be shared by so many.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sachs |first=Jeffrey D. |title=The End of Poverty: Economic Possibilities for Our Time |year=2005 |publisher=Penguin Press |isbn=978-1-59420-045-8 |pages=30–32}}</ref> Others claimed that powerful nations with large economies were not doing enough to help improve the rapidly evolving economies of the [[Third World]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Stiglitz |first=Joseph E. |title=Globalization and Its Discontents |journal=World Development |volume=28 |issue=6 |year=2000 |pages=1074–1076 |doi=10.1016/S0305-750X(00)00031-4|doi-broken-date=12 July 2025 }}</ref> Developing countries faced many challenges, including the scale of the task to be surmounted, rapidly growing populations, and the need to protect the environment, along with the associated costs.<ref>{{cite book |last=Collier |first=Paul |title=The Bottom Billion: Why the Poorest Countries are Failing and What Can Be Done About It |year=2007 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-531145-7 |pages=40–42}}</ref>

Secondly, disease threatened to destabilize many regions of the world. Viruses such as [[West Nile virus|West Nile]] and [[Avian influenza]] continued to spread quickly and easily.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Reiter |first=Paul |title=West Nile Virus in Europe: Understanding the Present to Gauge the Future |journal=Eurosurveillance |volume=15 |issue=10 |year=2010 |doi=10.2807/ese.15.10.19508-en |pages=5–6|pmid=20403311 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Avian Influenza A (H5N1) Infection in Humans |url=https://www.cdc.gov/flu/avianflu/h5n1-people.htm |website=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) |date=25 April 2023 |access-date=4 September 2024}}</ref> In poor nations, [[malaria]] and other diseases affected the majority of the population.<ref>{{cite web |title=Malaria |url=https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria |website=World Health Organization (WHO) |access-date=4 September 2024}}</ref> Millions were infected with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, which was becoming an [[AIDS in Africa|epidemic in southern Africa]] and around the world.<ref>{{cite web |title=Global HIV & AIDS Statistics |url=https://www.unaids.org/en/resources/fact-sheet |website=UNAIDS |access-date=4 September 2024}}</ref>

Increased [[globalization]], specifically [[Americanization]], was also occurring. While not necessarily a threat, it was causing [[Anti-Western sentiment|anti-Western]] and [[Anti-Americanism|anti-American]] feelings in parts of the world, especially in the Middle East.<ref>{{cite book |last=Chomsky |first=Noam |title=Hegemony or Survival: America's Quest for Global Dominance |year=2003 |publisher=Metropolitan Books |isbn=978-0-8050-7400-0 |pages=45–47}}</ref> English was quickly becoming the global language, with people who did not speak it becoming increasingly disadvantaged.<ref>{{cite book |last=Crystal |first=David |title=English as a Global Language |year=1997 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-59247-5 |pages=13–15}}</ref>

[[Terrorism]], dictatorship, and the spread of [[nuclear weapons]] were also issues requiring immediate attention. Dictators such as [[Kim Jong-il]] in North Korea continued to lead their nations toward the development of nuclear weapons.<ref>{{cite book |last=Cha |first=Victor D. |title=The Impossible State: North Korea, Past and Future |year=2012 |publisher=Ecco |isbn=978-0-06-199850-8 |pages=20–22}}</ref> The fear existed that not only were terrorists already attempting to obtain nuclear weapons, but that they had already acquired them.<ref>{{cite book |last=Allison |first=Graham |title=Nuclear Terrorism: The Ultimate Preventable Catastrophe |year=2004 |publisher=Henry Holt and Co. |isbn=978-0-8050-7852-7 |pages=15–18}}</ref>

== The end of the modern era ==
The end of this era most likely will come once either [[Artificial Super Intelligence|ASI]] becomes the driving force in global political economies or when human driven [[climate change]] and environmental decay ''<u>permanently</u>'' after earth's geology forcing an end to a '''modern industrial confidence.''' Another popular theory on what could happen to make a new era is post scarcity which could mean that a new era would hold a <big>near infinite</big> amount of clean energy like <u>[[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion or]] [[power grids]],</u> the '''elimination''' of <u>poverty</u>, ''<u>physical</u>'' wealth as a status symbol, and a traditional labor market. With some good things like poverty being eliminated come bad things like ASI which could mean artificial intelligence replacing pure human though and creativity which is already being demonstrated in [[Artificial intelligence|AI]] "art".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Future Timeline {{!}} Technology {{!}} Singularity {{!}} Future Events {{!}} 2025 {{!}} 2050 {{!}} 2100 |url=https://www.futuretimeline.net/ |access-date=2026-10-27 |website=www.futuretimeline.net}}</ref>

The following [[Outline (list)|outline]] is provided as an overview of and topical guide to technology:

'''[[Technology]]''' &ndash; collection of tools, including machinery, modifications, arrangements and procedures used by humans. [[Engineering]] is the discipline that seeks to study and design new technology. Technologies significantly affect human as well as other animal species' ability to control and adapt to their natural environments.

== Branches of technology ==

* '''[[Outline of aerospace|Aerospace]]''' &ndash; flight or transport above the surface of the Earth.
** [[Outline of space exploration|Space exploration]] &ndash; the physical investigation of the space more than 100&nbsp;km above the Earth by either crewed or uncrewed spacecraft.
** [[General aviation]]
** [[Aeronautics]]
** [[Astronautics]]
** [[Aerospace engineering]]
* '''[[Outline of applied physics|Applied physics]]''' &ndash; physics which is intended for a particular technological or practical use. It is usually considered as a bridge or a connection between "pure" physics and engineering.
* '''[[Outline of agriculture|Agriculture]]''' &ndash; cultivation of plants, animals, and other living organisms.
** [[Outline of fishing|Fishing]] &ndash; activity of trying to catch fish. Fish are normally caught in the wild. Techniques for catching fish include hand gathering, spearing, netting, angling and trapping.
*** [[Outline of fisheries|Fisheries]] &ndash; a fishery is an entity engaged in raising or harvesting fish which is determined by some authority to be a fishery. According to the FAO, a fishery is typically defined in terms of the "people involved, species or type of fish, area of water or seabed, method of fishing, class of boats, purpose of the activities or a combination of the foregoing features".
*** [[Outline of the fishing industry|Fishing industry]] &ndash;  industry or activity concerned with taking, culturing, processing, preserving, storing, transporting, marketing or selling fish or fish products. It is defined by the FAO as including recreational, subsistence and commercial fishing, and the harvesting, processing, and marketing sectors.
** [[Outline of forestry|Forestry]] &ndash; art and science of tree resources, including plantations and natural stands. The main goal of forestry is to create and implement systems that allow forests to continue a sustainable provision of environmental supplies and services.
** [[List of organic gardening and farming topics|Organic gardening and farming]]
** [[List of sustainable agriculture topics|Sustainable agriculture]]
* '''[[Outline of communication|Communication]]'''
** [[Outline of books|Books]]
** [[Outline of telecommunication|Telecommunication]] &ndash; the transfer of information at a distance, including signaling, telegraphy, telephony, telemetry, radio, television, and data communications.
*** [[Outline of radio|Radio]] &ndash; Aural or encoded telecommunications.
*** [[Outline of the Internet|Internet]] &ndash; the global system of interconnected computer networks that use the standard Internet Protocol Suite (TCP/IP).
*** [[Technology of television]]
**** [[Outline of television broadcasting|Television broadcasting]] &ndash; Visual and aural telecommunications.
* '''[[Outline of computing|Computing]]''' &ndash; any goal-oriented activity requiring, benefiting from, or creating computers. Computing includes designing and building hardware and software systems; processing, structuring, and managing various kinds of information; doing scientific research on and with computers; making computer systems behave intelligently; creating and using communications and entertainment media; and more.
** [[Outline of computer engineering|Computer engineering]] &ndash;  discipline that integrates several fields of electrical engineering and computer science required to develop computer systems, from designing individual microprocessors, personal computers, and supercomputers, to circuit design.
*** [[Outline of computers|Computers]] &ndash; general purpose devices that can be programmed to carry out a finite set of arithmetic or logical operations. Since a sequence of operations can be readily changed, computers can solve more than one kind of problem.
** [[Outline of computer science|Computer science]] &ndash; the study of the theoretical foundations of information and computation and of practical techniques for their implementation and application in computer systems.
*** [[Outline of artificial intelligence|Artificial intelligence]] &ndash; intelligence of machines and the branch of computer science that aims to create it.
**** [[Natural language processing]]
**** [[Outline of object recognition|Object recognition]] &ndash; in computer vision, this is the task of finding a given object in an image or video sequence.
*** [[Outline of cryptography|Cryptography]] &ndash; the technology to secure communications in the presence of third parties.
*** [[Outline of human–computer interaction|Human-computer interaction]]
** [[Outline of information technology|Information technology]] &ndash; the acquisition, processing, storage and dissemination of vocal, pictorial, textual and numerical information by a microelectronics-based combination of computing and telecommunications.
** [[Outline of software engineering|Software engineering]] &ndash; the systematic approach to the development, operation, maintenance, and retirement of computer software.
*** [[Outline of computer programming|Programming]] &ndash; the process of designing, writing, testing, debugging, and maintaining the source code of computer programs.
*** [[Outline of software development|Software development]] &ndash; development of a software product, which entails computer programming (process of writing and maintaining the source code), but also encompasses a planned and structured process from the conception of the desired software to its final manifestation.
*** [[Outline of web design and web development|Web design and web development]]
** [[Outline of software|Software]] &ndash; one or more computer programs and data held in the storage of the computer for one or more purposes. In other words, software is a set of programs, procedures, algorithms and its documentation concerned with the operation of a data processing system.
*** [[Outline of free software|Free software]] &ndash; software that can be used, studied, and modified without restriction.
*** [[Outline of search engines|Search engines]] &ndash; information retrieval systems designed to help find information stored on a computer system.
** [[Outline of the Internet|Internet]] &ndash; the global system of interconnected computer networks that use the standard Internet Protocol Suite (TCP/IP).
*** [[World Wide Web]]
** Computer industry
*** [[Outline of Apple Inc.|Apple Inc.]] &ndash; manufacturer and retailer of computers, hand-held computing devices, and related products and services.
*** [[Outline of Google|Google]] &ndash; Google Inc. and its Internet services including Google Search.
* '''[[Outline of construction|Construction]]''' &ndash; building or assembly of any physical structure.
* '''[[Outline of design|Design]]''' &ndash; the art and science of creating the abstract form and function for an object or environment.
** [[Outline of architecture|Architecture]] &ndash; the art and science of designing buildings.
* '''[[Outline of electronics|Electronics]]''' &ndash; Electronics comprises the physics, engineering, technology and applications that deal with the emission, flow and control of electrons in vacuum and matter.
* '''[[Outline of energy|Energy]]''' &ndash; In physics, energy is the quantitative property that must be transferred to an object in order to perform work on, or to heat, the object.
**[[Outline of energy development|Energy development]] &ndash; ongoing effort to provide abundant, efficient, and accessible energy resources through knowledge, skills, and construction.
** [[Outline of energy storage|Energy storage]] &ndash; the storage of a form of energy that can then be used later.
** [[Outline of nuclear technology|Nuclear technology]] &ndash; the technology and application of the spontaneous and induced reactions of atomic nuclei.
** [[Outline of wind energy|Wind energy]] &ndash; wind energy is the use of wind to provide the mechanical power through wind turbines to turn electric generators and traditionally to do other work, like milling or pumping.
** [[Outline of solar energy|Solar energy]] &ndash; Solar energy is radiant light and heat from the Sun that is harnessed using a range of ever-evolving technologies such as solar heating, photovoltaics, solar thermal energy, solar architecture, molten salt power plants and artificial photosynthesis.
* '''[[Outline of engineering|Engineering]]''' &ndash; the application of science, mathematics, and technology to produce useful goods and systems.
**[[Outline of chemical engineering|Chemical engineering]] &ndash; the technology and application of chemical processes to produce useful materials.
** [[Outline of computer engineering|Computer engineering]] &ndash; Computer engineering (CE) is a branch of engineering that integrates several fields of computer science and electronic engineering required to develop computer hardware and software.
** [[Outline of control engineering|Control engineering]] &ndash; Control engineering or control systems engineering is an engineering discipline that applies automatic control theory to design systems with desired behaviors in control environments.
** [[Outline of electrical engineering|Electrical engineering]] &ndash; the technology and application of electromagnetism, including electricity, electronics, telecommunications, computers, electric power, magnetics, and optics.
** [[Climate engineering]] &ndash;  the large-scale manipulation of a specific process central to controlling Earth's climate for the purpose of obtaining a specific benefit.
** [[Outline of software engineering|Software engineering]] &ndash; the technology and application of a systematic approach to the development, operation, maintenance, and retirement of computer software.
* '''[[Outline of firefighting|Firefighting]]''' &ndash; act of extinguishing fires. A firefighter fights fires to prevent destruction of life, property and the environment. Firefighting is a professional technical skill.
* '''[[Outline of forensic science|Forensic science]]''' &ndash; application of a broad spectrum of sciences to answer questions of interest to a legal system. This may be in relation to a crime or a civil action.
* '''[[Outline of health sciences|Health]]'''
** [[Outline of biotechnology|Biotechnology]] &ndash; applied biology that involves the use of living organisms and bioprocesses in engineering, technology, medicine and other fields requiring [[bioproducts]].
** [[Outline of ergonomics|Ergonomics]] &ndash; the study of designing equipment and devices that fit the human body, its movements, and its cognitive abilities.
* '''[[Outline of hydrology|Hydrology]]''' &ndash; The study of the movement, distribution, and quality of water on Earth and other planets, including the hydrologic cycle, water resources and environmental watershed sustainability.
* '''[[Outline of industry|Industry]]''' &ndash; production of an economic good or service.
** [[Outline of automation|Automation]] &ndash; use of machinery to replace human labor.
** [[Outline of industrial machinery|Industrial machinery]]
** [[Outline of machines|Machines]] &ndash; devices that perform or assist in performing useful work.
** [[Outline of manufacturing|Manufacturing]] &ndash; use of machines, tools and labor to produce goods for use or sale. The term may refer to a range of human activity, from handicraft to high tech, but is most commonly applied to industrial production, in which raw materials are transformed into finished goods on a large scale.
** [[Outline of robotics|Robotics]] &ndash; deals with the design, construction, operation, structural disposition, manufacture and application of robots.
*** [[Outline of object recognition|Object recognition]]
* '''[[Outline of information science|Information science]]'''
** [[Outline of cartography|Cartography]] &ndash; the study and practice of making maps. Combining science, aesthetics, and technique, cartography builds on the premise that reality can be modeled in ways that communicate spatial information effectively.
** [[Outline of library science|Library science]] &ndash; technology related to libraries and the information fields.
* '''[[Outline of military science and technology|Military science]]''' &ndash; the study of the technique, psychology, practice and other phenomena which constitute war and armed conflict.
* '''[[Outline of mining|Mining]]''' &ndash; extraction of mineral resources from the earth.
* '''[[Outline of nanotechnology|Nanotechnology]]''' &ndash; The study of manipulating matter on an atomic and molecular scale. Generally, nanotechnology deals with structures sized between 1 and 100 nanometre in at least one dimension, and involves developing materials or devices possessing at least one dimension within that size.
* '''[[Outline of prehistoric technology|Prehistoric technology]]''' &ndash; technologies that emerged before recorded history (i.e., before the development of writing).
* '''[[Quantum technology]] '''
* '''[[Outline of sustainability|Sustainability]]''' &ndash; capacity to endure. In ecology, the word describes how biological systems remain diverse and productive over time. Long-lived and healthy wetlands and forests are examples of sustainable biological systems. For humans, sustainability is the potential for long-term maintenance of well-being, which has environmental, economic, and social dimensions.
* '''[[Outline of transport|Transport]]''' &ndash; the transfer of people or things from one place to another.
** [[Outline of rail transport|Rail transport]] &ndash;  means of conveyance of passengers and goods by way of wheeled vehicles running on rail tracks consisting of steel rails installed on sleepers/ties and ballast.
** [[Outline of vehicles|Vehicles]] &ndash; mechanical devices for transporting people or things.
*** [[Outline of automobiles|Automobiles]] &ndash; human-guided powered land-vehicles.
*** [[Outline of bicycles|Bicycles]] &ndash; human-powered land-vehicles with two or more wheels.
*** [[Outline of motorcycling|Motorcycles]] &ndash; single-track, engine-powered, motor vehicles. They are also called motorbikes, bikes, or cycles.
*** Vehicle components
**** [[Outline of tires|Tires]] &ndash; ring-shaped coverings that fit around wheel rims

=== Media about the history of technology ===
* ''[[Connections (British documentary)|Connections]]'' &ndash; documentary television series and 1978 book ("Connections" based on the series) created, written, and presented by science historian James Burke. It took an interdisciplinary approach to the history of science and invention and demonstrated how various discoveries, scientific achievements, and historical world events were built from one another successively in an interconnected way to bring about particular aspects of modern technology. There were 3 seasons produced, and they aired in 1978, 1994, and 1997. 
* ''[[The Day the Universe Changed]]'' &ndash; documentary television series written and presented by science historian James Burke, originally broadcast in 1985 by the BBC. The series' primary focus is on the effect of advances in science and technology on western society in its philosophical aspects. Ran for one season, in 1986.

== Hypothetical technology ==
Potential technology of the future includes:

[[Hypothetical technology]]
* [[Femtotechnology]] &ndash; hypothetical term used in reference to structuring of matter on the scale of a femtometer, which is 10−15 m. This is a smaller scale in comparison to nanotechnology and picotechnology which refer to 10−9 m and 10−12 m respectively. Work in the femtometer range involves manipulation of excited energy states within atomic nuclei (see nuclear isomer) to produce metastable (or otherwise stabilized) states with unusual properties.
