WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Pasquale's Angel
======================================================================

{{Short description|1994 novel by Paul J. McAule}}
{{Infobox book
| image             = Firenze-Florenz-Florence at night from Piazzale Michelangelo.jpg
| author            = [[Paul J. McAuley]]
| isbn              = 0-575-05489-1
| pub_date          = March 31, 1994
| name              = Pasquale's Angel
| caption           = Night view of [[Florence]].
| language          = English
| country           = United Kingdom
| genre             = [[Novel]]<br>[[Science fiction]]<br>[[Uchronia]]
| publisher         = [[Victor Gollancz Ltd]]
| pages             = 320
| awards            = [[Sidewise Award for Alternate History]] (1995)
}}
'''''Pasquale's Angel''''' is an alternate [[Uchronia|history]] [[novel]] by [[Paul J. McAuley]], published in 1994. Set in early 16th-century [[Florence]], the novel depicts a world where [[Leonardo da Vinci]] has abandoned art for engineering, triggering an [[Industrial Revolution|industrial revolution]] during the [[Italian Renaissance]]. The story follows Pasquale, a young painter and pupil of [[Rosso Fiorentino|Giovanni Battista Rosso]], who, after the murders of the artist [[Raphael]] and his assistant [[Giulio Romano]], partners with the political journalist [[Niccolò Machiavelli|Machiavelli]] to investigate. Their inquiry uncovers a broad conspiracy against the backdrop of tensions with [[Spain]] and a [[Girolamo Savonarola|Savonarolan]] uprising.

Pasquale’s Angel combines [[steampunk]]-inspired alternate [[Uchronia|history]], [[detective fiction]], [[fantasy]], and coming-of-age elements. The novel includes references to [[Sherlock Holmes]], [[Edgar Allan Poe]], and [[Frankenstein in popular culture|Frankenstein cinema]], while exploring themes of [[Progress#Scientific progress|scientific]] and [[Technological change|technological progress]] and its societal consequences.

The novel received positive critical reception and won the 1995 [[Sidewise Award for Alternate History|Sidewise Award]] for Best Long Form Alternate History. Its companion short story, ''The Temptation of Dr. Stein'', set in the same universe, won the [[British Fantasy Award|British Fantasy Award for Best Short Story]] in the same year.

== Description ==

=== Setting ===
[[File:Map_of_Italy_(1494)-fr.svg|left|thumb|Map of the [[Italian Peninsula]] at the time of the story.]]
The [[point of divergence]] in this alternate [[Uchronia|history]] is [[Leonardo da Vinci]]’s career choice.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Domis |first=Benoît |date=1998 |title=Les Conjurés de Florence |trans-title=Pasquale's Angel |url=https://www.noosfere.org/livres/niourf.asp?numlivre=-318369 |journal=Galaxies |language=fr |issue=9 |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref> Forty years before the novel’s events,<ref name=":1">{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=58}}</ref> following the assassination of [[Lorenzo de' Medici|Lorenzo de’ Medici]]<ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=372}}</ref>—killed in a [[Pazzi conspiracy|plot]] orchestrated by the [[Pope Sixtus IV|Pope]]—Leonardo abandons painting to focus on [[engineering]]. His inventions and rediscoveries, including rocket-launching cannon, [[tank]]s, and [[Greek fire]], enabled the [[Republic of Florence]] to defeat the armies of [[Rome]] and [[Venice]].<ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=243}}</ref> During the brief reign of Lorenzo’s successor, his brother [[Giuliano de' Medici|Giuliano]], a purge of dissenters takes place before a revolt<ref name=":1" /> removes his dynasty from power.<ref group="Note">The [[House of Medici|Medici]] were at that time banished from the Florentine Republic.</ref><ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=165}}</ref> Leonardo, known as the “Grand Engineer,” established a university where inventions such as [[Aeolipile|Hero’s engine]], the [[printing press]], and a [[Steam engine|steam-powered automobile]] (''vaporetto'') were developed or improved, initiating an early [[Industrial Revolution|industrial revolution]]<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Trudel |first=Jean-Louis |date=2000 |title=The SF Site Featured Review: Pasquale's Angel |url=https://www.sfsite.com/05b/pa81.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241215180312/https://www.sfsite.com/05b/pa81.htm |archive-date=2024-12-15 |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref> and creating a division between craftsmen (the “artificers”<ref name=":0" />) and artists.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Paul J. McAuley interview conducted at ConFuse 98 |url=https://www.lysator.liu.se/lsff/confuse00/Paul_J_McAuley_interview.html |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref>

In this alternate world, [[Christopher Columbus]], serving the Tuscan Republic rather than Spain, discovers the [[Antilles|Friendly Islands of the New World]].<ref name=":1" /> [[Amerigo Vespucci]] establishes peaceful trade relations with [[Moctezuma II|Moctezuma]]’s [[Aztec Empire]].<ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=167}}</ref> [[Tobacco]], [[Natural rubber|rubber]], and [[Cannabis (drug)|marijuana]] become common consumer goods. Ten years before the novel’s events,<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=493}}</ref> the Spanish fleet under Admiral [[Hernán Cortés|Cortés]] attacks Florence and its New World colonies.<ref name=":4">{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=64}}</ref><ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=463}}</ref> Despite Florence’s victory, aided by the Grand Engineer’s use of [[Greek fire]],<ref name=":4" /> the city undergoes political instability following the fall of the government led by [[Piero Soderini|Pietro Soderini]],<ref group="Note">Until then, lifelong [[gonfaloniere]], Soderini had committed suicide during the Spanish attack</ref><ref name=":1" /> before regaining stability. Meanwhile, the Grand Engineer gradually retreats to the tower at the center of his university, reducing his involvement in public life.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Killheffer |first=Robert K. J |date=1996 |title=Books |url=https://archive.org/details/Fantasy_Science_Fiction_v090n02_1996-02_Lenny_Silv3r_dtsg0318/page/n26 |journal=[[The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction]] |volume=90 |issue=537 |pages=28–34 |issn=0024-984X |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref>

=== Summary ===

==== Part one: The Feast of Saint Luke ====
[[File:Stefanoussi1894.JPG|thumb|[[Niccolò Machiavelli]], political journalist at the ''Gazette of Florence.'']]
Set in 1519,<ref name=":3" /> the novel follows eighteen-year-old Pasquale de Cione Fiesole, a student of painter [[Rosso Fiorentino|Giovanni Battista Rosso]].<ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=27}}</ref> Aspiring to gain recognition by painting an angel,<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last1=McAuley |first1=Paul J. |url=https://www.elbakin.net/fantasy/roman/les-conjures-de-florence-792 |title=Les Conjurés de Florence |date=March 29, 2005 |publisher=Editions Gallimard |isbn=978-2-07-030286-4 |language=fr |trans-title=Pasquale's Angel |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref> Pasquale currently undertakes small commissions amid the rising status of artisans in Florence. At the annual [[Luke the Evangelist|Saint Luke]]’s Mass, a key event for the city’s painters, he witnesses a heated exchange between [[Salaì|Salai]], a member of the Grand Engineer’s circle, and the visiting artist [[Raphael]], who is in Florence ahead of Pope [[Pope Leo X|Leo X]]’s arrival.<ref name=":0" /> Pasquale’s account attracts the attention of [[Niccolò Machiavelli]], a former government official turned journalist, who invites him to illustrate an article on the incident. Soon after, a murder occurs at {{Interlanguage link|Palazzo Taddei|lt=Palazzo Taddei|fr|Palazzo Taddei}}, where Raphael is staying. Machiavelli and Pasquale discover the body of [[Giulio Romano]], one of Raphael’s disciples, in a locked tower room, holding a model of a [[Leonardo's aerial screw|propeller-driven flying machine]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=May 20, 2010 |title=Pasquale's Angel by Paul J. McAuley |url=https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/paul-j-mcauley/pasquales-angel/ |access-date=May 27, 2025 |website=Kirkus Reviews}}</ref>

The signal operator reveals Giulio had bribed him to stay in the tower, though the reason is unknown. The captain of the militia discreetly assigns Machiavelli to investigate. Machiavelli enlists Pasquale’s help in questioning suspects, including [[Michelangelo]] and Raphael,<ref name=":7" /> who hints at a conspiracy but offers little information. That night, the pair observe someone signaling from the tower and follow him, [[Gianfrancesco Penni|Giovanni Francesco]], another of Raphael’s students, to the villa of [[Paul Giustiniani|Paolo Giustiniani]], a Venetian mystic linked to Marsilio Ficino and rumored to practice sorcery.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ficino |first=Marsilio |title=Three Books on Life |date=2019 |publisher=Arizona Center for Medieval and Renaissance Studies |isbn=9780866988223}}</ref> They witness Giustiniani kill Francesco with a poisoned smoke bomb during an argument. Machiavelli and Pasquale intervene too late to save him, but Pasquale retrieves a small glass-framed image Giustiniani tried to destroy. After evading the villa’s guards, they escape.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Henry |first1=Tom |title=Late Raphael |last2=Joannides |first2=Paul |date=2013 |publisher=Thames & Hudson |isbn=978-0500970492}}</ref>

===== Part two: On Earth as in Heaven =====
[[File:Raffaello,_autoritratto_con_un_amico_01.jpg|left|thumb|[[Raphael]] (left) with a friend, possibly his student [[Giulio Romano]].]]
As Pope [[Pope Leo X|Leo X]] arrives in Florence to public celebration, Pasquale and Machiavelli reflect on the previous night and examine the recovered image, which depicts Giustiniani participating in a [[Black Mass|black mass]]. Machiavelli theorizes that Giovanni Francesco had evidence of Giustiniani’s involvement in occult rituals and was blackmailing him for unknown reasons.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bradburne |first=James |title=Hidden voices : discovering the Buonomini di San Martino |date=2011 |publisher=Giunti |isbn=9788809774162 |oclc=819996870}}</ref> They are then visited by [[Mona Lisa|Mona Lisa Giocondo]], wife of government official [[Francesco del Giocondo]] and secret lover of Raphael, who offers Machiavelli a purse of florins to support the investigation.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kemp |first1=Martin |title=Mona Lisa: The People and the Painting |last2=Pallanti |first2=Giuseppe |date=2017 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0198749905}}</ref> That evening, they use the funds to consult Doctor Pretorius, a physician rumored to practice [[black magic]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Allen |first=Joanne |title=Transforming the Church Interior in Renaissance Florence |date=2022 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9781108985659 |doi=10.1017/9781108985659}}</ref> He confirms that Raphael has no connection to Giustiniani.

After escaping an ambush by Giustiniani’s men, who had discovered their presence at his villa, Pasquale and Machiavelli head to the [[Palazzo Vecchio|Palazzo della Signoria]] to inform Raphael. At the palace, Raphael is dining with Pope Leo X and his entourage after a presentation by the Grand Engineer, who unveiled an invention that creates images by [[Photography|capturing light]].<ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=134}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> Upon arrival, they learn Raphael has been poisoned via the rim of his wine glass,<ref name=":7" /> suggesting Machiavelli was the intended target. The palace is then attacked by Giustiniani’s men using stilts and toxic smoke bombs. In the chaos, Pasquale is separated from Machiavelli but is rescued by servants of Palazzo Taddei and brought to their master, {{Interlanguage link|Taddeo Taddei|lt=Signor Taddei|fr|Taddeo Taddei}}. Accompanied by his astrologer [[Gerolamo Cardano|Girolamo Cardano]] and Cardinal [[Pope Clement VII|Jules de Medici]], Taddei questions Pasquale and informs him that Raphael’s body has been stolen.<ref name=":15">{{Cite book |last=Grafton |first=Anthony |title=Cardano's Cosmos: The Worlds and Works of a Renaissance |date=2001 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0674006706}}</ref> The kidnapper demands Pasquale’s release in exchange. To avoid a diplomatic crisis with Rome, Pasquale is chloroformed and taken to the [[Ponte Vecchio]] for the exchange.<ref name="Partner 1990">{{Cite book |last=Partner |first=Peter |title=The Pope's Men: The Papal Civil Service in the Renaissance |date=1990 |publisher=Clarendon Press |isbn=978-0198219958}}</ref>
[[File:Ponte_Vecchio_at_dusk_1.JPG|thumb|The [[Ponte Vecchio]] bridge over the [[Arno]] river.]]
There, the bridge is set ablaze by the [[Ciompi Revolt|''ciompi'']], rebellious workers incited by the Savonarolists.{{refn|The disciples of [[Girolamo Savonarola|Savonarola]], who had taken refuge in Spain<ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=269}}</ref> after establishing a brief {{Interlanguage link|Theocracy in Florence|lt=theocracy in Florence|fr|Théocratie à Florence}} several years earlier.|group=Note}}<ref name=":16">{{Cite book |last=Najemy |first=John M |title=A History of Florence, 1200 - 1575 |date=2008 |publisher=Wiley-Blackwell |isbn=978-1405182423}}</ref> Amid the confusion, Pasquale regains consciousness and escapes with help from his master, Rosso, who appears with his pet monkey, Ferdinand. Rosso leads him to a building where Salai, the Savonarolist monk Fra Perlata, and a captive Machiavelli—about to be tortured—are being held.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Villari |first=Pasquale |title=Life and Times of Girolamo Savonarola |date=2005 |publisher=Kessinger Publishing |isbn=978-1419180354}}</ref> The conspirators transport their captives across the [[Arno]] by [[barge]], but an unexpected attack by Giustiniani’s men causes confusion, allowing Pasquale to escape with Rosso’s help.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hibbert |first=Christopher |title=Florence: The Biography of a City |date=1994 |publisher=Penguin |isbn=978-0140166446}}</ref>

==== Part three: The Interrupted Measure ====
After reaching the Arno’s bank, Pasquale, Rosso, and the monkey Ferdinand spend the night outside Florence. Rosso reveals that Giustiniani orchestrated the conspiracy to obtain the Grand Engineer’s latest invention—a flying machine he intended to sell to Spain.<ref name=":17">{{Cite book |last=Galluzzi |first=Paolo |title=The Art of Invention - Leonardo and Renaisance Engineers |date=1999 |publisher=Giunti |isbn=978-8809014824}}</ref> Acting on Salai’s instructions, Giulio Romano stole the model during a visit to the Grand Engineer’s tower. Fearing discovery by the secret police, Romano attempted to send the model to Rosso using the semaphore at Palazzo Taddei. Ferdinand was meant to retrieve it but, possibly mistaking Romano for an intruder, accidentally killed him. The model remained in the tower, later discovered by Machiavelli and Pasquale.<ref name=":18">{{Cite book |last=Scribner |first=Robert W |title=By Robert W. Scribner - The German Reformation |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |edition=2nd}}</ref> Giustiniani demanded the model, but Giovanni Francesco attempted to negotiate independently and was killed.<ref name=":19">{{Cite book |last=Burke |first=Peter |title=The Italian Renaissance: Culture and Society in Italy |date=2014 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=9780691162409 |edition=3rd}}</ref> The conspirators then distanced themselves from Giustiniani, who continued plotting Raphael’s assassination and allied with Savonarolist factions financially backed by Spain.<ref name=":16" />
[[File:Leonardo_self.jpg|left|thumb|[[Leonardo da Vinci]], the Great Engineer.]]
The next morning, Pasquale finds that Rosso has died by suicide. Determined to end the violence, he decides to return the model to the Grand Engineer.<ref name=":7" /> He retrieves it from Machiavelli’s home before Giustiniani’s agents can.<ref name=":19" /> To access the Grand Engineer’s tower, Pasquale hides among cadavers bound for dissection. Discovered and arrested by Salai, he is confined in a room filled with skulls, and the model is confiscated. The Grand Engineer later frees him upon learning of Salai’s betrayal—delivering the model to Giustiniani.<ref name=":16" /> With the Grand Engineer’s support, Pasquale and Machiavelli seek assistance from Signor Taddei to launch an assault on Giustiniani’s villa. The plan involves Pasquale infiltrating the villa under the pretense of possessing the Grand Engineer’s secret notes, necessary to operate the flying machine.<ref name=":17" /> The aim is to recover both the model and Raphael’s body while distracting Giustiniani long enough for Taddei’s forces—equipped with the Grand Engineer’s inventions—to strike.<ref name=":18" />

Inside the villa, Pasquale finds Giustiniani performing an occult ritual around Raphael’s body, accompanied by Salai, a Spanish emissary sent for the model, and a captured Machiavelli.<ref name=":20">{{Cite book |last=Trexler |first=Richard |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.7591/j.ctvv415gs |title=Public Life in Renaissance Florence |date=1980 |publisher=Cornell University Press |jstor=10.7591/j.ctvv415gs |isbn=978-1-5017-2027-7 |access-date=May 28, 2025}}</ref> During negotiations, the villa is attacked prematurely due to a betrayal by Cardano, the astrologer secretly aligned with the Savonarolists. The building is set ablaze,<ref name=":16" /> and in the chaos, Pasquale and Machiavelli escape, though the model is destroyed. The Spanish emissary's death provides Spain with a pretext to declare war on Florence.<ref name=":21">{{Cite book |last=Kamen |first=Henry |title=Spain, 1469-1714: A Society of Conflict |date=2005 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0582784642 |edition=3rd}}</ref> As the republic prepares for conflict and offers Machiavelli a return to political office, Pasquale departs for the New World.<ref name=":20" />

== Characters ==

=== Painters and their circle ===
[[File:Thomas_Couture-Anselm_Feuerbach_1852.JPG|thumb|Portrait of the young painter [[Anselm Feuerbach]] (1852).]]
A significant number of characters in the novel are painters. The protagonist, Pasquale de Cione Fiesole, is an 18-year-old painter from [[Fiesole]] who aspires to depict the angel expelling [[Fall of man|Adam and Eve from Eden]]. His experiences during the investigation with Machiavelli shape his artistic vision.<ref name=":16" /> Pasquale is a student of [[Rosso Fiorentino|Giovanni Battista Rosso]],<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=Clute |first=John |date=1994 |title=Feeling Safe to Look |url=https://archive.org/details/Interzone_085_1994-07/page/n57 |journal=[[Interzone (magazine)|Interzone]] |issue=85 |pages=59–60 |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref> a 24-year-old painter nostalgic for a time when artists held greater influence in Florence before being overshadowed by pyrotechnicians.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Barolsky |first=Paul |title=Why Mona Lisa Smiles and Other Tales by Vasari |date=1991 |publisher=Penn State University Press |isbn=978-0271007199}}</ref> Financial hardship drives Rosso to join the Spanish plot to steal the Grand Engineer’s flying machine. Wracked with guilt, he ultimately dies by suicide.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cropper |first=Elizabeth |title=The Ideal of Painting: Pietro Testa's Dusseldorf Notebook |date=1984 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0691040219}}</ref> Rosso is accompanied by Ferdinand, his tame [[macaque]], named after [[Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria|Ferdinand of Aragon]], who dies during the final attack on Giustiniani’s villa when Giustiniani kills him, mistaking him for a demon.<ref name=":21" />

The novel includes several prominent painters of the ''[[Cinquecento]]'', notably [[Raphael|Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino]], widely regarded as the leading painter of his era. He is dispatched to Florence in advance of the pope’s visit to help ease longstanding tensions between the Tuscan Republic and Rome, dating back to a war<ref name=":0" /> forty years earlier. During the annual [[Luke the Evangelist|Saint Luke]]’s Mass, a major event for Florentine painters, Raphael is publicly insulted by Salai. He later visits the Grand Engineer’s tower and is subsequently poisoned during a banquet with the pope.<ref name=":22">{{Cite book |last1=Hartt |first1=Frederick |title=History of Italian Renaissance art |last2=Wilkins |first2=David |date=2010 |publisher=Pearson |isbn=978-0205705818 |edition=7th}}</ref> Among his disciples, [[Giulio Romano]], implicated in the conspiracy, is accidentally killed by the monkey Ferdinand while attempting to deliver the flying model to Rosso. Another student, [[Giovanni Francesco Straparola|Giovanni Francesco]], threatens to expose Paolo Giustiniani’s alleged involvement in occult practices after Romano’s failure but is killed by Giustiniani.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Shearman |first=John |title=Raphael's cartoons in the collection of Her Majesty the Queen, and the tapestries for the Sistine Chapel |date=1972 |publisher=Phaidon |isbn=978-0714814506}}</ref> A third student, Baverio, assists Pasquale by providing critical information during the investigation.<ref name=":22" />

The novel also features [[Michelangelo|Michelangelo Buonarroti]], depicted as Raphael’s rival,<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last=Ecken |first=Claude |date=1998 |title=Les critiques de Bifrost : Les Conjurés de Florence |trans-title=Bifrost's reviews: The Conjurers of Florence |url=https://www.belial.fr/blog/les-conjures-de-florence |journal=Bifrost |language=fr |pages=8 |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref> who accuses him of appropriating his artistic ideas.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hibbard |first=Howard |title=Michelangelo |date=2007 |publisher=Folio Society}}</ref> Another notable figure of the [[Florentine Renaissance]], the elderly painter [[Piero di Cosimo]], is regarded by Pasquale as his “secret master.” Piero is portrayed as a reclusive figure who, following a journey to the land of the [[Huichol|Wixárika]] in the [[New World]], habitually consumes ''[[Peyote|híkuri]]'', a psychoactive plant, in pursuit of visionary experiences.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Hallucinogens and Shamanism |date=1973 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0195016505}}</ref> Piero advises Pasquale to contact Nicolaus Copernicus to gain entry to the Grand Engineer’s tower, based on their prior acquaintance. He lives with Pelashil, his servant and a member of the Wixárika people, who considers him a ''mara'akame'' ([[Shamanism|shaman]]) and has become his disciple.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schaefer |first=Stacy B. |date=2023 |title=Huichol shamanism: traditional wisdom in a modern world |url=https://www.scielo.cl/pdf/bmchap/v28n1/0718-6894-bmchap-28-01-83.pdf |journal=Boletín del Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=83–102 |doi=10.56522/BMCHAP.0060010280003 |archive-date= |access-date=May 28, 2025}}</ref> She also assists Pasquale and Machiavelli during their escape from Giustiniani’s villa in the final stages of the narrative.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Martines |first=Lauro |title=April Blood: Florence and the Plot against the Medici |date=2004 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0195176094}}</ref>

Several Florentine painters are referenced in the novel. [[Pontormo]] is briefly mentioned through his twelve-year-old student, Bernardo, who is fatally struck by a ''vaporetto'' ([[Steam engine|steam-powered]] vehicle) at the beginning of the narrative, on the eve of Saint Luke’s Day.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Strehlke |first1=Carl Brandon |title=Pontormo, Bronzino, and the Medici |last2=Cropper |first2=Elizabeth |date=2004 |publisher=Philadelphia Museum of Art |isbn=9780876331804}}</ref> [[Andrea del Sarto]], the former teacher of Rosso and a prominent member of the Florentine painters’ brotherhood, also appears.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Brooks |first1=Julian |title=Andrea del Sarto: The Renaissance Workshop in Action |last2=Allen |first2=Denise |last3=Salomon |first3=F |date=2015 |publisher=J. Paul Getty Museum |isbn=978-1606064382}}</ref> His student, [[Andrea Sguazella|Andrea Squazella]], is portrayed as a friend of the protagonist, Pasquale.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Baxandall |first=Michael |title=Painting and Experience in Fifteenth-Century Italy: A Primer in the Social History of Pictorial Style |date=1988 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0192821447 |edition=2nd}}</ref>

=== Journalists and circles of power ===
[[File:Leonardo_da_Vinci,_artist,_thinker_and_man_of_science;_(1898)_(14779194171).jpg|left|thumb|Copy of Leonardo da Vinci's ''[[Mona Lisa]]'' by Raphael.]]
''Pasquale's Angel'' explores themes of media and political power in an alternate-history version of Florence. A central character is [[Niccolò Machiavelli]], portrayed as a former Secretary of the Ten ([[Ministry of defence|Minister of Defense]]) under the administration of [[Piero Soderini|Pietro Soderini]]. Following the fall of Soderini's government during the war with Spain, Machiavelli was imprisoned for two years in the dungeons of the [[Bargello|Palazzo del Bargello]], accused of attempting to restore Medici influence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wolfgang |first=Marvin |date=1990 |title=Crime and Punishment in Renaissance Florence |url=https://scholarlycommons.law.northwestern.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=6668&context=jclc |journal=Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology |volume=81 |issue=3 |pages=567–584 |doi=10.2307/1143848 |jstor=1143848 |access-date=May 28, 2025|url-access=subscription }}</ref> After his release, he became a political columnist for the ''Florence Gazette'', a tabloid publication based in the former premises of the publisher [[Vespasiano da Bisticci]].<ref group="Note">Who went bankrupt due to his refusal to adopt new [[Printing press|typographic presses]].</ref> Despite a tendency toward excessive [[drinking]], Machiavelli plays a key role in the investigation into the deaths of Romano and Raphael.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Machiavelli and Renaissance Political Thought |url=https://dantesisofo.com/machiavelli-and-renaissance-political-thought/ |access-date=May 28, 2025 |website=Dante Sisofo}}</ref> Other figures associated with the press include Pietro Aretino ([[Pietro Aretino]]), the director of the ''Florence Gazette'',<ref name=":5" /> and [[Giambattista Gelli]]a, a former cobbler and revolutionary known for his [[pamphlet]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rossi |first=Daniella |date=2007 |title=Humanism and the Renaissance |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25834052 |journal=The Year's Work in Modern Language Studies |volume=69 |pages=476–490 |jstor=25834052 |access-date=May 28, 2025}}</ref>

Another prominent character is Signor Taddei, a merchant and owner of the Palazzo Taddei, where the character Romano is killed. Taddei is depicted as maintaining strong connections with the Vatican and is advised by Girolamo Cardano ([[Gerolamo Cardano|Jerome Cardan]]), a mathematician and astrologer who is later revealed to be secretly aligned with the Savonarolists.<ref name=":15" /> Cardano escapes at the end of the novel, taking Salai with him. The narrative also includes [[Mona Lisa|Mona Lisa Giocondo]],<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last=Millet |first=Gilbert |date=2005 |title=Lectures : Les Conjurés de Florence |trans-title=Readings: Pasquale's Angel |url=https://www.noosfere.org/livres/niourf.asp?numlivre=-318369 |journal=Galaxies |language=fr |issue=36 |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref> portrayed as the wife of [[Lisa del Giocondo|Francesco Giocondo]], Secretary of the Ten of War in the Florentine government, and the secret lover of Raphael.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Leader |first=Anne |title=This Day in History: June 15 |url=https://www.italianartsociety.org/2017/06/lisa-gherardini-aka-mona-lisa-the-wife-of-florentine-cloth-merchant-francesco-del-giocondo-was-born-on-15-june-1479-in-florence/?utm_source=chatgpt.com |access-date=May 28, 2025 |website=Italian Art Society}}</ref>

=== Engineers and magicians ===
[[File:Leonardo_Salai.JPG|thumb|Sketch of Salai by Leonardo da Vinci.]]
One of the central figures in McAuley’s alternate history is [[Leonardo da Vinci]], referred to as the Grand Engineer. As the narrative's point of divergence,<ref name=":2" /> he is portrayed as the inventor who initiated an industrial revolution that enabled Florence to surpass other European powers.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kemp |first=Martin |title=Leonardo da Vinci: The Marvellous Works of Nature and Man |date=2007 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0199207787}}</ref> In the novel, he is depicted as an aging, contemplative figure who has retired to a self-constructed tower at the center of the city,<ref name=":8" /> where he continues his research. His latest invention, a flying machine, becomes the focal point of the conspiracy.<ref name=":7" /> Leonardo’s former student and companion, Giacomo Caprotti—known as [[Salaì|Salai]]—is portrayed as gaining increasing control over both Leonardo and his university.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zöllner |first=Frank |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fq8IHuJIKmoC |title=Leonardo Da Vinci, 1452-1519 |date=2000 |publisher=Taschen |isbn=9783822859797 |access-date=May 28, 2025}}</ref> Salai plays a key role in the plot to acquire the flying machine, alternating his allegiance between Giustiniani and the Savonarolists. He is eventually captured and taken from Florence by Cardano and the Savonarolists. [[Jacopo Saltarelli|Jacopo]], Leonardo’s guard, appears as a loyal figure who assists Pasquale in gaining the Grand Engineer’s trust, motivated by his opposition to Salai. The narrative also includes [[Nicolaus Copernicus]]<ref name=":2" /> (''Niklas Koppernigk''), described as a [[Prussia]]n scientist credited with the [[Heliocentrism|heliocentric]] model of the solar system.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gingerich |first=Owen |title=The Book Nobody Read: Chasing the Revolutions of Nicolaus |date=2005 |publisher=Penguin Books}}</ref> Resentful over the appropriation of his work,{{refn|Initially imperfect, as they required a series of artificial adjustments ([[Deferent and epicycle|epicycles]]) to be applied to the movement of celestial bodies.<ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=|pp=330–331}}</ref>|group=Note}} he is portrayed as embittered and reclusive, primarily teaching his theories to Prussian students in taverns in exchange for payment or alcohol.

Another character in the novel is Benozzo Berni, an artificer and distant relative of the satirical poet [[Francesco Berni]]. He collaborates with Rosso and Pasquale to illuminate the façade of a bank on the [[Piazza della Signoria]] during festivities in honor of the pope. The narrative also features Paolo Giustiniani ([[Paul Giustiniani]]), a Venetian-born writer and mystic. Formerly a priest, he is depicted as knowledgeable in occult practices and influenced by [[Marsilio Ficino]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Celenza |first=Christopher S |title=The Lost Italian Renaissance: Humanists, Historians, and Latin's Legacy |date=2006 |publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |isbn=978-0801883842}}</ref> Initially leading the conspiracy to sell the Grand Engineer’s flying machine to Spain, he later pursues an independent agenda.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Walker |first=D.P |title=Spiritual and Demonic Magic: From Ficino to Campanella (Magic in History) |date=2001 |publisher=The Pennsylvania State University Press |isbn=978-0271020457}}</ref> Giustiniani dies during the final assault on his villa while attempting to invoke the archangel [[Uriel]] through a sacrificial ritual involving Raphael’s body. The poisoning of Raphael is carried out by one of Giustiniani’s associates, known as the “redhead,” who is later killed by Pelashil during the villa assault. The character of Doctor Pretorius also appears in the novel. He is a physician and occultist from whom Machiavelli obtains information. Reputed for conducting experiments on corpses, he is portrayed as a figure with extensive knowledge of events in Florence.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Connelly |first=Frances S |title=The Grotesque in Western Art and Culture: The Image at Play |date=2012 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1107011250}}</ref> In the related [[short story]] ''The Temptation of Dr. Stein'', it is revealed that Pretorius once attempted to resurrect a body using [[electricity]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vial |first=Éric |date=2000 |title=Lectures : Aventures lointaines |trans-title=Readings: Faraway Adventures |url=https://www.noosfere.org/livres/niourf.asp?numlivre=-327477 |journal=Galaxies |language=fr |issue=16 |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref> and to create a being called the “Virgin of the Seas” from assembled body parts.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Montillo |first=Roseanne |title=The Lady and Her Monsters: A Tale of Dissections, Real-Life Dr. Frankensteins, and the Creation of Mary Shelley's Masterpiece |date=2013 |publisher=William Morrow Paperbacks |isbn=978-0062025838}}</ref>

=== Men of the church ===
The novel includes several clerical figures. Pope [[Pope Leo X|Leo X]],<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |last=Barrett |first=David |date=April 2, 1994 |title=Review: A Florentine world turned upside down |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg14219193-700-review-a-florentine-world-turned-upside-down/ |access-date=May 27, 2025 |website=New Scientist}}</ref> son of former Florentine leader [[Lorenzo de' Medici|Lorenzo de’ Medici]], visits Florence in an attempt to reconcile the Tuscan Republic with Rome. However, he departs soon after the assassination of Raphael and the outbreak of a Savonarolist uprising.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hibbert |first=Christopher |title=The House of Medici: Its Rise and Fall |date=1999 |publisher=Mariner Books |isbn=978-0688053390}}</ref> He is accompanied by his cousin, Cardinal [[Giulio de' Medici (died 1598)|Giulio de’ Medici]], who engages in discussions with Signor Taddei, Girolamo Cardano, and Pasquale following Raphael’s death.<ref name="Partner 1990"/> The narrative also features Fra Perlata, a Savonarolist monk involved in the conspiracy linked to Spain.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Weinstein |first=Donald |title=Savonarola and Florence: Prophecy and Patriotism in the Renaissance |date=1970 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0691051840}}</ref>

== Genesis of the novel ==
[[File:Paul_McAuley_2005.JPG|left|thumb|[[Paul J. McAuley]] in 2005.]]
When writing ''Pasquale's Angel'', [[Paul J. McAuley]] was an established science fiction author, having received the [[Philip K. Dick Award]] in 1989 for ''Four Hundred Billion Stars''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Title: Four Hundred Billion Stars |url=https://www.isfdb.org/cgi-bin/title.cgi?1902 |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref> Following the publication of ''Red Dust'' in 1993,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Title: Red Dust |url=https://www.isfdb.org/cgi-bin/title.cgi?1332 |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref> he began work on ''Pasquale's Angel'', inspired by the idea of transposing [[Renaissance]] characters into a [[Victorian era|Victorian]]-like setting.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=Futures that Work: Paul J. McAuley Interview |url=https://www.hoopoes.com/sf/iv_mcauley.html |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref>

McAuley’s interest in [[Leonardo da Vinci]] and his machines<ref name=":12" /> forms the point of divergence in the novel’s alternate history. Setting the story several decades after this divergence required extensive research to ensure historical plausibility. He spent six months consulting contemporary sources,<ref name=":3" /> benefiting from the emergence of early [[Biography|biographies]] of da Vinci.<ref name=":12" /> This research enabled him to incorporate machines based on authentic designs and inventions, such as 13th-century floating mills from Paris,<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |last=Gevers |first=Nick |date=1999 |title=Hard Science, Radical Imagination : An Interview with Paul J. McAuley |url=https://www.infinityplus.co.uk/nonfiction/intpmca.htm |access-date=May 27, 2025 |website=[[Infinity Plus]]}}</ref> as well as numerous historical figures. Only the protagonist, Pasquale, born after the divergence, and a few [[Stock character|minor characters]] are fictional.<ref name=":12" />

Among the historical figures featured in the novel, the character of Machiavelli posed a particular challenge for the author.<ref name=":3" /> Originally intended to appear briefly as a means for Pasquale to access the crime scene, Machiavelli ultimately became central to the plot, despite McAuley’s efforts to reduce his role, including scenes in which the character is tortured.<ref name=":3" /> The detective storyline involving Machiavelli forms a core element of the novel,<ref name=":13" /> although McAuley considers Pasquale’s artistic quest—the search for the angel he aims to paint, which also inspired the novel’s original title, ''Pasquale’s Angel''—to be the primary focus.<ref name=":3" />

== Reception ==

=== Critical reception ===
The novel was generally well received upon its 1994 release, and its reputation grew steadily thereafter. In 2005, seven years after the French translation by Olivier Deparis, literary critic Gilbert Millet described it as a “classic of alternate [[Uchronia|history]].”<ref name=":10" /> In 1995, ''[[Publishers Weekly]]'' called it “ambitious and often brilliant,” praising its “masterfully constructed [[chiaroscuro]] world”<ref>{{Cite web |date=1995 |title=Fiction Book Review: Pasquale's Angel by Paul J. McAuley |url=https://www.publishersweekly.com/978-0-688-14154-7 |access-date=May 27, 2025 |website=[[Publishers Weekly]]}}</ref> and noting that Machiavelli is portrayed as “Machiavellian even in everyday conversation.” Canadian author [[Jean-Louis Trudel]] wrote that McAuley “takes [[steampunk]] to an unprecedented level,”<ref name=":2" /> highlighting the novel’s attention to detail, from “a Machiavelli playing the [[Sherlock Holmes]] of the Renaissance” to “a [[Cameo appearance|cameo]] of a Polish canon named Copernicus.” Although Trudel questioned the plausibility of an industrialized Florence and noted occasional narrative slowdowns, he concluded that the book “will delight lovers of the unexpected juxtapositions offered by steampunk: the roaring engines of modernity transposed into old alleyways, and the lost heroes of our history brushing shoulders with characters born of the author’s imagination.” ''[[Kirkus Reviews]]'' was more reserved, describing the work as “meticulously constructed, with a fascinating blend of real and imaginary historical characters,” but critiquing its “grim, hermetic nature” and reluctance to engage the reader.<ref name=":7" /> ''[[New Scientist]]'' offered one of the most negative appraisals, lamenting the emphasis on the detective plot and “political complexities” at the expense of setting and mysticism, and faulting an “awkward writing style, littered with verbless sentences […], [[Dependent clause|subordinate clauses]] attached to the wrong noun […], [[cliché]]s […] and repetitions.”<ref name=":11" />

In the [[Francophonie|French-speaking world]], the novel received a generally positive reception and contributed to Paul J. McAuley’s recognition among French readers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=McAULEY Paul J. |url=https://www.etonnants-voyageurs.com/McAULEY-Paul-J.html |access-date=May 27, 2025 |website=Étonnants Voyageurs |language=fr}}</ref> French author [[Claude Ecken]] praised the novel for striking “the right balance in his collage of historical elements and speculative shifts,” describing it as “delightful, clever, full of references” and able to appeal to both general literature readers and fans of quality science fiction.<ref name=":9" /> The French fantasy site ''[[Elbakin.net]]'' rated ''Pasquale’s Angel'' 8/10, noting that although the connection between the two parallel plots—the detective mystery and Pasquale’s artistic quest—was somewhat weak, “the plots themselves are captivating” and the detailed style effectively immerses readers in the alternate Florence.<ref name=":6" /> Gilbert Millet of ''Galaxies'' described the novel as “lively and mischievous,” offering a “festive alternate history, rich in winks and twists,” and considered it “more imaginative than The [[The Da Vinci Code|Da Vinci Code]].”<ref name=":10" /> Among more critical responses, Laurent Deneuve from ActuSF found the pacing too rapid in the middle section, which he felt diminished reader engagement with the plot.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Deneuve |first=Laurent |date=September 20, 2018 |title=Les Conjurés de Florence |trans-title=Pasquale's Angel |url=https://www.actusf.com/detail-d-un-article/les-conjures-de-florence |access-date=May 27, 2025 |language=fr}}</ref> Conversely, Belgian writer {{Interlanguage link|Karine Gobled|lt=Karine Gobled|fr|Karine Gobled}} regarded the novel as “accessible and exciting to read,” recommending it as an introduction to alternate history,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vincent |first=Jérôme |date=September 27, 2018 |title=Interview de Bertrand Campeis et Karine Gobled pour le Guide de l'Uchronie |trans-title=Interview with Bertrand Campeis and Karine Gobled for the Guide to Uchronia |url=https://www.actusf.com/detail-d-un-article/interview-de-bertrand-campeis-et |access-date=May 27, 2025 |language=fr}}</ref> while Jérôme Vincent of ActuSF included it among the ten essential works of the genre.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vincent |first=Jérôme |date=October 31, 2017 |title=Dix uchronies incontournables |trans-title=Ten must-read alternate histories |url=https://www.actusf.com/detail-d-un-article/10-uchronies-incontournables |access-date=May 27, 2025 |language=fr}}</ref>

=== Awards ===
''Pasquale’s Angel'' received the 1995 [[Sidewise Award for Alternate History|Sidewise Award]] for long-form alternate history.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sidewise: Past Winners and Finalists |url=https://www.uchronia.net/sidewise/complete.html#pagebox |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref> In the same year, it was a finalist for the [[Arthur C. Clarke Award]], placed 29th in the [[Locus Award for Best Science Fiction Novel|Locus Awards for Best Science Fiction Novel]], and was nominated for the [[British Fantasy Award|August Derleth Award for Best Fantasy Novel]], the [[Hugo Award for Best Novel]], and the [[Grand prix de l'Imaginaire|Grand Prix de l’Imaginaire]] (foreign novel category).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Title: Pasquale's Angel |url=https://www.isfdb.org/cgi-bin/title.cgi?1414 |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref>

The related [[short story]] ''Dr. Pretorius’s Temptation'', which explores the actions of Doctor Pretorius ten years prior to the events of ''Pasquale’s Angel'', won the [[British Fantasy Award|British Fantasy Award for Best Short Story]] in 1995 and was nominated for the 1996 [[Sidewise Award for Alternate History|Sidewise Award]] (short form).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Title: The Temptation of Dr Stein |url=https://www.isfdb.org/cgi-bin/title.cgi?43030 |access-date=May 27, 2025}}</ref>

== Analysis ==

=== A work at the crossroads of literary genres ===
[[File:Vis_aerienne_Luc_Viatour.jpg|thumb|The Great Engineer's [[Leonardo's aerial screw|flying invention]], coveted by all.]]
The ''Pasquale's Angel'' by McAuley is a novel that spans multiple [[literary genre]]s, primarily classified as alternate history. This subgenre of [[science fiction]], originating in the 19th century with [[Charles Renouvier]], involves the "fictional reconstruction of history, recounting events as they might have happened."<ref>{{Cite web |title=uchronie |trans-title=uchronia |url=https://www.larousse.fr/dictionnaires/francais/uchronie/10910032 |access-date=May 28, 2025 |website=Larousse |language=fr}}</ref> Alternate history is defined by a divergence from a specific historical point,<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |last1=Bozzetto |first1=Roger |last2=Goimard |first2=Jacques |title=Science-fiction : Uchronies, le passé revisité |trans-title=Science fiction: Alternate histories, revisiting the past |url=https://www.universalis.fr/encyclopedie/science-fiction/8-uchronies-le-passe-revisite/ |access-date=May 28, 2025 |website=[[Encyclopædia Universalis]] |language=fr}}</ref> creating a new narrative explored by the author. In ''Pasquale's Angel'', the point of divergence is twofold: [[Lorenzo de' Medici|Lorenzo de’ Medici]], rather than his brother [[Giuliano de' Medici|Giuliano]], is assassinated during the [[Pazzi conspiracy]] in 1478;<ref name=":5" /> and [[Leonardo da Vinci]] chooses to focus on engineering instead of art.<ref name=":0" /> These changes set in motion a transformation of the world depicted in the novel, leading to an industrialized Florence that dominates the West and the New World approximately four decades later.<ref name=":0" />

The industrial setting of ''Pasquale's Angel'' aligns the novel with [[steampunk]], a subgenre of alternate history that envisions a fictional past where the [[Industrial Revolution]] occurred earlier than in reality.<ref name=":14" /> Benoît Domis compares the novel to [[Tim Powers]]' ''[[The Anubis Gates]]'',<ref name=":0" /> a foundational work in the genre, while [[John Clute]] draws parallels with ''[[The Difference Engine]]'' by [[William Gibson]] and [[Bruce Sterling]].<ref name=":8" /> However, since steampunk is typically set in [[Victorian England]]<ref name=":14" /> rather than [[Italian Renaissance|Renaissance Italy]], classifying McAuley’s novel as steampunk is debated. Writer [[Ned Beauman]] considers it more accurately an example of clockpunk, a subgenre that places modern technological developments in the [[Renaissance]] period.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Beauman |first=Ned |date=March 16, 2007 |title=New new worlds : the glory of sci-fi sub-genres |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/booksblog/2007/mar/16/newnewworldsthegloryofsc |access-date=May 28, 2025 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> ''[[Kirkus Reviews]]'' describes the novel as “oldmasterpunk,” combining steampunk with references to old master painters featured among the characters.<ref name=":7" />

''Pasquale's Angel'' can also be classified as a [[Detective fiction|detective novel]],<ref name=":9" /> with its plot centered on the investigation of two murders—the killing of Raphael’s assistant and the subsequent poisoning of Raphael himself—pursued by Pasquale and Machiavelli. The narrative is driven by multiple twists in the crime mystery.<ref name=":10" /> The novel incorporates elements of the [[supernatural]] and [[fantasy]], including events linked to the occultist Giustiniani that often have rational explanations, as well as [[mysticism]] associated with the [[Shamanism|shamanic]] practices of the [[Huichol|Wixárika]] [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Amerindians]],<ref name=":6" /> introduced to Pasquale by his former mentor Piero di Cosimo and the Wixárika woman Pelashil. Additionally, through Pasquale’s artistic development and personal growth, the novel can also be regarded as a [[Bildungsroman]].<ref name=":9" />

=== A tribute to popular culture ===
[[File:Sherlock_Holmes_Portrait_Paget.jpg|left|thumb|[[Sherlock Holmes]], McAuley's inspiration for the character of Machiavelli.]]
Writing ''Pasquale's Angel'' allowed McAuley to include numerous references to popular literature and cinema,<ref name=":12" /> especially within the [[supernatural]]-[[Detective fiction|detective genre]].<ref name=":0" /> A prominent comparison is drawn between Machiavelli and [[Sherlock Holmes]], the detective created by [[Arthur Conan Doyle]].<ref name=":0" /> Like Holmes, Machiavelli applies observation and deduction to investigate crimes, functioning as an early form of private detective.<ref name=":12" /> [[Literary criticism|Literary critic]] Robert K. J. Killheffer highlights Machiavelli’s principle to Pasquale—“Once all materially inadmissible hypotheses have been discarded, it is among those that remain, however improbable they may seem, that the true solution must be sought.”—as an inverted reference to Holmes’s famous maxim.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Doyle |first=Arthur Conan |url=https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/La_Marque_des_quatre/VI |title=Le Signe des quatre |date=1896 |publisher=Hachette |location=Paris |pages=81 |language=fr |trans-title=[[The Sign of the Four]] |access-date=May 28, 2025}}</ref><ref name=":5" /> The partnership between Machiavelli and Pasquale parallels the Holmes-[[Dr. Watson|Watson]] dynamic,<ref name=":0" /> with an experienced investigator mentoring a less experienced assistant in crime-solving techniques.<ref name=":6" />

Parallels can be drawn between ''Pasquale's Angel'' and other detective works, particularly those of [[Edgar Allan Poe]]. The adventures of Poe’s character [[C. Auguste Dupin|Auguste Dupin]], a private investigator in [[Paris]] during the [[July Monarchy]], are reflected in the novel’s plot, especially in “the nature of the mysteries posed and the manner of solving them,” according to critic Benoît Domis.<ref name=":0" /> The murder of Giulio Romano, Raphael’s assistant, resembles the killings in Poe’s ''[[The Murders in the Rue Morgue]]'',<ref name=":0" /> where victims are found in a locked room under seemingly inexplicable circumstances until the detective reveals the unusual perpetrator. Additionally, the discovery of the crime’s motive—an insignificant model found at the scene and later placed in plain sight—echoes ''[[The Purloined Letter]]'',<ref name=":0" /> in which a stolen letter is hidden by its ordinary appearance and obvious placement, eluding detection. Machiavelli’s fondness for alcohol also alludes to Poe’s reputed alcoholism; McAuley has described both men as “drunken journalists.”<ref name=":3" />
[[File:BrideofFrankenstein13B.jpg|thumb|[[Doctor Septimus Pretorius|Dr. Pretorius]] ([[Ernest Thesiger]], right) in the film ''[[Bride of Frankenstein|The Bride of Frankenstein]]''.]]
The novel has been compared to the works of [[Gaston Leroux]], who combines detective fiction with the fantastic, and to ''[[The Name of the Rose]]'' by [[Umberto Eco]], whose monk-detective [[William of Baskerville]] shares investigative qualities with Machiavelli.<ref name=":9" /> McAuley, however, clarifies that this similarity arises from the shared Holmesian influence on both novels rather than direct inspiration from Eco’s work.<ref name=":3" /> Another reference to popular culture appears in the character of Doctor Pretorius, taken from [[James Whale]]’s 1935 film ''[[Bride of Frankenstein|The Bride of Frankenstein]]''.<ref>{{Cite news |last=McAuley |first=Paul J |date=August 21, 1999 |title=The monster and the mad scientist |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/1999/aug/21/books.guardianreview7 |access-date=May 28, 2025 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> In the film, loosely based on [[Mary Shelley]]’s ''[[Frankenstein|Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus]]'', the [[mad scientist]] [[Doctor Septimus Pretorius|Septimus Pretorius]] conducts experiments to animate inanimate flesh, paralleling McAuley’s portrayal. The character is further developed in McAuley’s short story ''The Temptation of Dr. Stein'', which incorporates elements from the [[golem]] legend<ref name=":6" />—an artificial being from [[Jewish mythology]] lacking free will and entirely subject to its master.

=== Reflection on scientific progress ===
In ''Pasquale's Angel'', McAuley, primarily a [[science fiction]] author, explores the theme of [[Progress#Scientific progress|scientific]] and [[Technological change|technological progress]],<ref name=":0" /> defined as an improvement in production methods through the refinement of machines and the mechanization of labor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Progrès |trans-title=Progress |url=https://www.cnrtl.fr/definition/progr%C3%A8s |access-date=May 28, 2025 |website=NRTL |language=fr}}</ref> In the novel, Leonardo da Vinci introduces innovative inventions that lead, as writer [[John Clute]] notes, to a transition “from organic life to industrial life ([[Gemeinschaft and Gesellschaft|from ''Gemeinschaft'' to ''Gesellschaft'']]<ref group="Note">That is, according to the work of [[Sociology|sociologist]] [[Ferdinand Tönnies]], from community to society, from a collective entity founded on reciprocal sentiments to a group of individuals bound by reasoning or calculation. According to Tönnies, the advent of the industrial era in the 19th century had as its main sociological consequence the transformation of humanity from a state of ''Gemeinschaft'', or community, to that of ''Gesellschaft'', or society.</ref>), from ad hoc technical creation to a feared engineering,” reflecting aspects of the 19th-century [[Industrial Revolution|industrial revolution]].<ref name=":8" /> McAuley<ref name=":3" /> also highlights the separation of art and technique as one of these developments.
{{Blockquote|text=This distinction between the activity of the artist and that of the engineer is apparent in da Vinci, but it did not exist before simply because it was not recognized. No one saw any real difference between the condition of the artist and that of the craftsman. It was the same thing: since there was no mass production, making frames for paintings was valued just as much as painting them, as an important aspect of the artist’s work. And if you look at the very old frames that surround Renaissance paintings, you’ll see what I mean. Learning how to make them was part of an artist’s training. Since then, we’ve experienced a specialization, and da Vinci embodies the first appearance of this modern dichotomy between art and science, which is why, in my opinion, we’re so fascinated by him.<ref name=":3" />}}
[[File:'The_Begum's_Fortune'_by_Léon_Benett_12.jpg|left|thumb|Stahlstadt, the industrial city of the ''Five Hundred Million of the Begum'' by Jules Verne.]]
John Clute observes that, unlike other alternate history novels such as ''[[Pavane (novel)|Pavane]]'' by [[Keith Roberts]], where characters appear isolated amid decline, societal change is central in McAuley’s work, with characters actively engaging with transformation.<ref name=":8" /> The theme of progress is therefore central to the novel. However, progress is not presented uncritically; ''Pasquale's Angel'' depicts the negative consequences of technological advancement, including pollution, social violence, and worker exploitation. According to critic Robert K. J. Killheffer,<ref name=":5" /> this serves as a critique of "the worst weaknesses of the [[Capitalism|capitalist]] system." Some characters, such as an old worker encountered by Pasquale and Machiavelli, express skepticism or hostility toward industrialization, reflecting concerns relevant to contemporary society:<ref name=":5" />
{{Blockquote|text=They say the artificers have given men the freedom to progress, but keeping up with the pace of their machines, men like me become less than beasts of burden: they work us as long as we can still stand, and when we collapse, they toss us aside.<ref>{{Harvsp|McAuley|2004|p=98}}</ref>}}
The [[dystopia]]n aspect of the novel is reinforced by the extreme centralization of power in the hands of a single figure, the Grand Engineer:
{{Blockquote|text=At the heart of the new Florence rises a vast building, the tower where old Leonardo lives in solitude with his catamite and his servants, like a kind of satanic anthropologist. This tower is the center of a vast network of communication relays. Like the sentient computer in ''[[The Difference Engine]]'', it is all eyes: through various openings, high above the dominated city, complex optical systems constantly monitor human lives, reduced to counters on a map.<ref name=":8" />}}
According to Benoît Domis, McAuley thus follows the continuity of his previous works by “once again raising the question of scientific responsibility. Can the artificers […] so easily take refuge behind an inevitable progress to avoid feeling guilty for the upheavals caused by their work? Who is responsible for the division of the city into two, between very wealthy merchants and a labor force that is very poor and deskilled by the wonders developed by da Vinci? Of course, Paul McAuley does not provide the answer, but his questions echo for a long time in the attentive reader’s mind: progress, yes, but for whom?<ref name=":0" />”

== Sequel project ==
In an interview published in August 1998 in Locus magazine, Paul J. McAuley announced plans for a sequel to ''Pasquale's Angel'', set one hundred years after the original novel.<ref>{{Cite web |title=P A U L J. M c A U L E Y : Recreating the Future |url=https://www.locusmag.com/1998/Issues/08/Mcauley.html |access-date=May 28, 2025 |website=Locus Online}}</ref> The sequel was intended to explore [[European colonization of the Americas]] under a more scientific context, with implications for slavery and the fate of indigenous peoples, potentially involving a “counterfactual [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]].”<ref>{{Cite book |last=Seed |first=David |title=Science Fiction: A Very Short Introduction |date=2011 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0199557455}}</ref> In December 1999, McAuley provided further details, stating the story would take place fifty years after ''Pasquale's Angel'' and follow a quest for the legendary [[Seven Cities of Gold|golden cities]] of Cibola across the Americas.<ref name=":13" /> However, the project was hindered by the publisher [[Victor Gollancz Ltd|Gollancz]], which retained rights to the original novel, preventing other publishers from releasing the sequel.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mendlesohn |first=Farah |title=Rhetorics of Fantasy |date=2008 |publisher=Wesleyan University Press |isbn=978-0819568687}}</ref> As a result, the sequel was ultimately abandoned.

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Plastic
======================================================================

{{short description|Material of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organic solids}}
{{Other uses}}
{{pp-semi-indef}}
{{Use American English|date=March 2021}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=September 2023}}
[[File:Plastic household items.jpg|thumb|upright=1.35|Household items made of various types of plastics]]
'''Plastics''' are a wide range of [[synthetic polymers|synthetic]] or [[Semisynthesis|semisynthetic]] materials composed primarily of [[polymer]]s. Their defining characteristic, [[Plasticity (physics)|plasticity]], allows them to be [[Injection moulding|molded]], [[Extrusion|extruded]], or [[Compression molding|pressed]] into a diverse range of solid forms. This adaptability, combined with a wide range of other properties such as low weight, durability, flexibility, chemical resistance, low toxicity, and low-cost production, has led to their widespread use around the world.<ref name="Ullmann Plastics, General Survey, 1. Definition, Molecular Structure and Properties">{{Ullmann |last1=Elias |first1=Hans-Georg |last2=Mülhaupt |first2=Rolf |title=Plastics, General Survey, 1. Definition, Molecular Structure and Properties |date=2015 |pages=1–69 |doi=10.1002/14356007.a20_543.pub2 |isbn=978-3-527-30385-4 }}</ref> While most plastics are produced from [[natural gas]] and [[petroleum]], a growing minority are produced from [[Renewable resource|renewable resources]] like [[polylactic acid]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Life Cycle of a Plastic Product |url=http://www.americanchemistry.com/s_plastics/doc.asp?CID=1571&DID=5972 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100317004747/http://www.americanchemistry.com/s_plastics/doc.asp?CID=1571&DID=5972 |archive-date=March 17, 2010 |access-date=July 1, 2011 |website=Americanchemistry.com |language=en}}</ref>

Between 1950 and 2017, 9.2 billion metric tons of plastic are estimated to have been made, with more than half of this amount being produced since 2004. In 2023 alone, preliminary figures indicate that over 400 million metric tons of plastic were produced worldwide.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2023-04-13 |title=Global plastic production with projections, 1950 to 2060 |url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/global-plastic-production-projections?form=MG0AV3 |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=Our World In Data |language=en}}</ref> If global trends in plastic demand continue, it is projected that annual global plastic production will exceed 1.3 billion tons by 2060.<ref name=":2" /> The primary uses for plastic include packaging, which makes up about 40% of its usage, and building and construction, which makes up about 20% of its usage.<ref name=Ull>{{cite book |doi=10.1002/14356007.a20_543.pub2 |chapter=Plastics, General Survey, 1. Definition, Molecular Structure and Properties |title=Ullmann's Encyclopedia of Industrial Chemistry |date=2015 |last1=Elias |first1=Hans-Georg |last2=Mülhaupt |first2=Rolf |pages=1–70 |isbn=978-3-527-30673-2 }}</ref>

The success and dominance of plastics since the early 20th century have had major benefits for mankind, ranging from medical devices to lightweight construction materials. The sewage systems in many countries rely on the resiliency and adaptability of [[polyvinyl chloride]]. It is also true that plastics are the basis of widespread environmental concerns,<ref>{{cite web |date=October 2020 |title=The environmental impacts of plastics and micro-plastics use, waste and pollution: EU and national measures |url=https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2020/658279/IPOL_STU(2020)658279_EN.pdf |website=europarl.europa.eu}}</ref> due to their slow decomposition rate in natural ecosystems. Most plastic produced has not been reused, thus the need for [[microplastic remediation]]. Some are unsuitable for reuse. Much ends up in [[landfill]]s or as [[plastic pollution]]. Particular concern focuses on [[microplastics]]. [[Marine plastic pollution]], for example, creates [[garbage patch]]es. Of all the plastic discarded so far, some 14% has been incinerated and less than 10% has been recycled.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |last=Environment |first=U. N. |date=October 21, 2021 |title=Drowning in Plastics – Marine Litter and Plastic Waste Vital Graphics |url=http://www.unep.org/resources/report/drowning-plastics-marine-litter-and-plastic-waste-vital-graphics |access-date=March 21, 2022 |website=UNEP - UN Environment Programme |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260130035935/https://www.unep.org/resources/report/drowning-plastics-marine-litter-and-plastic-waste-vital-graphics |archive-date=2026-01-30 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In developed economies, about a third of plastic is used in packaging and roughly the same in buildings in applications such as [[piping]], [[plumbing]] or [[vinyl siding]].<ref name="Applications" /> Other uses include automobiles (up to 20% plastic<ref name="Applications" />), furniture, and toys.<ref name="Applications" /> In the developing world, the applications of plastic may differ; 42% of India's consumption is used in packaging.<ref name="Applications" /> Worldwide, about 50&nbsp;kg of plastic is produced annually per person, with production doubling every ten years.

The world's first fully synthetic plastic was [[Bakelite]], invented in New York in 1907 by [[Leo Baekeland]],<ref name="Landmark">{{cite web|last1=American Chemical Society National Historic Chemical Landmarks|title=Bakelite: The World's First Synthetic Plastic|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/bakelite.html|access-date=February 23, 2015}}</ref> who coined the term ''plastics''.<ref name="Edgar and Edgar 2009">{{Cite book | vauthors = Edgar D, Edgar R |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_9WGar3yxsAC&q=Baekeland+coined&pg=PA11 |title=Fantastic Recycled Plastic: 30 Clever Creations to Spark Your Imagination|publisher=Sterling Publishing Company, Inc. |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60059-342-0 |via=Google Books}}</ref> Dozens of different types of plastics are produced today, such as [[polyethylene]], which is widely used in [[product packaging]], and [[polyvinyl chloride]] (PVC), used in construction and pipes because of its strength and durability. Many chemists have contributed to the [[materials science]] of plastics, including [[Nobel laureate]] [[Hermann Staudinger]], who has been called "the father of [[polymer chemistry]]", and [[Herman Francis Mark|Herman Mark]], known as "the father of [[polymer physics]]".<ref name="Teegarden 2004">{{Cite book | vauthors = Teegarden DM |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0qFQ5OuKoy8C&q=%22father+of+polymer%22&pg=PA58 |title=Polymer Chemistry: Introduction to an Indispensable Science |publisher=NSTA Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-87355-221-9 |via=Google Books}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The word ''[[wikt:plastic|plastic]]'' derives from the [[Ancient Greek]] {{lang|grc|πλαστικός}} ({{lang|grc-Latn|plastikos}}), meaning "capable of being shaped or molded," which itself comes from {{lang|grc|πλαστός}} ({{lang|grc-Latn|plastos}}), meaning "molded" or "formed."<ref>{{cite web |title=Plastikos |script-title=grc:πλαστι^κ-ός |url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/cgi-bin/ptext?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.04.0057%3Aentry%3D%2383506 |access-date=July 1, 2011 |website=Henry George Liddell, Robert Scott, A Greek–English Lexicon}}</ref> In modern usage, the word ''plastic'' most commonly refers to the solid synthetic products of [[petrochemical]]-derived manufacturing.<ref>{{cite web |title=Plastic |url=https://www.etymonline.com/search?q=plastic |access-date=July 29, 2021 |website=Online Etymology Dictionary |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260227122746/https://www.etymonline.com/search?q=plastic |archive-date=2026-02-27 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The word ''plasticity'', as a noun, specifically refers to the deformability of the materials used in the manufacture of plastics. Plasticity allows molding, [[plastic extrusion|extrusion]], or [[compression molding|compression]] into a variety of shapes, including films, fibers, plates, tubes, bottles, and boxes, among many others. In [[materials science]], plasticity also has a more technical definition, describing the nonreversible change in form of solid substances when subjected to external forces. However, this definition extends beyond the scope of this article.{{cn|date=July 2025}}

== Structure ==
{{See also|Polymer}}Most plastics contain [[Organic compound|organic]] polymers.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BnccCgAAQBAJ&q=most+plastics+contain+organic+compounds&pg=PA52|title=General Chemistry| vauthors = Ebbing D, Gammon SD |date=2016|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=978-1-305-88729-9|language=en}}</ref> The vast majority of these polymers are formed from chains of carbon atoms, with or without the attachment of oxygen, nitrogen or sulfur atoms. These chains comprise many [[repeat unit|repeating units]] formed from [[monomer]]s. Each polymer chain consists of several thousand repeating units. The [[backbone chain|backbone]] is the part of the chain that is on the ''main path'', linking together a large number of repeat units. To customize the properties of a plastic, different molecular groups called [[side chains]] hang from this backbone; they are usually attached to the monomers before the monomers themselves are linked together to form the polymer chain. The structure of these side chains influences the properties of the polymer.{{cn|date=July 2025}}

==Classifications==
Plastics are usually classified by their chemical structure of the polymer's backbone and side chains. Important groups classified in this way include the [[acrylyl group|acrylics]], [[polyester]]s, [[silicones]], [[polyurethanes]], and [[halocarbon|halogenated plastics]]. Plastics can be classified by the chemical process used in their synthesis, such as [[condensation reaction|condensation]], [[polyaddition]], and [[cross-link]]ing.<ref>{{cite web |title=Classification of Plastics |url=http://dwb.unl.edu/Teacher/NSF/C06/C06Links/qlink.queensu.ca/~6jrt/chem210/Page3.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071215124919/http://dwb.unl.edu/Teacher/NSF/C06/C06Links/qlink.queensu.ca/~6jrt/chem210/Page3.html |archive-date=December 15, 2007 |access-date=July 1, 2011 |website=Joanne and Steffanie's Plastics Web Site |language=en}}</ref> They can also be classified by their [[physical properties]], including [[hardness]], [[density]], [[tensile strength]], [[thermal resistance]], and [[glass transition temperature]]. Plastics can additionally be classified by their resistance and reactions to various substances and processes, such as exposure to organic solvents, [[oxidation]], and [[ionizing radiation]].<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Kent R |title=Periodic Table of Polymers |url=http://www.pcn.org/Technical%20Notes%20-%20Periodic%20Table%20of%20Polymers.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080703034726/http://www.pcn.org/Technical%20Notes%20-%20Periodic%20Table%20of%20Polymers.htm |archive-date=July 3, 2008 |website=Plastics Consultancy Network |language=en}}</ref> Other classifications of plastics are based on qualities relevant to manufacturing or product design for a particular purpose. Examples include [[thermoplastics]], [[thermosetting polymer|thermosets]], [[conductive polymers]], [[biodegradable plastics]], [[engineering plastic]]s and [[elastomer]]s.

===Thermoplastics and thermosetting polymers===
[[File:Melted plastic.jpg|thumb|upright=0.75|The plastic handle of a kitchen utensil, deformed by heat. This behavior, in which the plastic resolidifies in a new shape after melting, is characteristic of thermoplastics.]] 
One important classification of plastics is the degree to which the chemical processes used to make them are reversible or not.

Thermoplastics do not undergo chemical change in their composition when heated and thus can be molded repeatedly. Examples include polyethylene (PE), [[polypropylene]] (PP), [[polystyrene]] (PS), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC).<ref>{{cite web |title=Composition and Types of Plastic |url=http://www.infoplease.com/ce6/sci/A0860420.html |website=Infoplease |language=en |access-date=September 29, 2009 |archive-date=October 15, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121015093623/http://www.infoplease.com/ce6/sci/A0860420.html }}</ref>

Thermosetting polymers, also known as thermosets, can melt and take shape only once: after they have solidified, they stay solid and retain their shape permanently.<ref>{{Cite book | vauthors = Gilleo K |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k_2qLoLA_tgC&q=%C2%A0Thermosets,+or+thermosetting+polymers,+can+melt+and+take+shape+only+once |title=Area Array Packaging Processes: For BGA, Flip Chip, and CSP |date=2004 |publisher=McGraw Hill Professional |isbn=978-0-07-142829-3 |language=en |via=Google Books}}</ref> If reheated, thermosets decompose rather than melt. Examples of thermosets include epoxy resin, polyimide, and Bakelite. The [[vulcanization]] of [[Natural rubber|rubber]] is an example of this process. Before heating in the presence of sulfur, natural rubber ([[polyisoprene]]) is a sticky, slightly runny material, and after vulcanization, the product is dry and rigid.

:{| class="wikitable skin-invert-image" style="text-align:left; font-size:90%; width:70%;"
|- class="hintergrundfarbe2" style="vertical-align:top"
| [[File:Polymerstruktur-engmaschig vernetzt.svg|center|upright=0.5]] [[Thermosets]] consist of closely cross-linked polymers. Cross-links are shown as red dots in the figure.
| [[File:Polymerstruktur-weitmaschig vernetzt.svg|center|upright=0.5]] [[Elastomers]] consist of wide-meshed cross-linked polymers. The wide mesh allows the material to stretch under tensile load.
| [[File:Polymerstruktur-teilkristallin.svg|center|upright=0.5]] [[Thermoplastics]] consist of non-crosslinked polymers, often with a semi-crystalline structure (shown in red). They have a glass transition temperature and are meltable.
|}

=== Commodity, engineering, and high-performance plastics ===

==== Commodity plastics ====
[[File:Plastics Summary.svg|class=skin-invert-image|right|250px|thumb|Chemical structures and uses of some common plastics]]
Commodity plastics or commodity polymers are plastics produced in high volumes for applications such as packaging, food containers, and household products, including both [[disposable product]]s and [[durable good]]s. In contrast to [[engineering plastic]]s, commodity plastics tend to be inexpensive to produce and exhibit relatively weak mechanical properties. Widely used commodity plastics include [[polyethylene]] (PE), [[polypropylene]] (PP), [[polystyrene]] (PS), [[polyvinyl chloride]] (PVC), [[poly(methyl methacrylate)]] (PMMA), and [[polyethylene terephthalate]] (PET). Products made from commodity plastics include [[disposable]] plates, [[disposable cup]]s, photographic and magnetic tape, clothing, reusable bags, medical trays, and seeding trays.<ref name=":4">{{cite book|last1=Kaiser|first1=Wolfgang|title=Kunststoffchemie für Ingenieure: Von der Synthese bis zur Anwendung|year=2011|publisher=Carl Hanser|isbn=978-3-446-43047-1|page=439}}</ref>

Approximately 80% of global plastic production includes commodity plastics, a type of plastics primarily chosen for their low cost and ease of manufacturing. These plastics are mass-produced and ubiquitous in packaging, food containers, and single-use items. Most commodity plastics are identifiable by their [[Resin identification code|Resin Identification Codes]] (RICs), a standardized numbering system developed by [[ASTM International]].
:[[File:Symbol Resin Code 01 PET.svg|class=skin-invert-image|35px]] [[Polyethylene terephthalate]] (PET or PETE)
:[[File:Symbol Resin Code 02 PE-HD.svg|class=skin-invert-image|35px]] [[High-density polyethylene]] (HDPE or PE-HD)
:[[File:Symbol Resin Code 03 PVC.svg|class=skin-invert-image|35px]] [[Polyvinyl chloride]] (PVC or V)
:[[File:Symbol Resin Code 04 PE-LD.svg|class=skin-invert-image|35px]] [[Low-density polyethylene]] (LDPE or PE-LD),
:[[File:Symbol Resin Code 05 PP.svg|class=skin-invert-image|35px]] [[Polypropylene]] (PP)
:[[File:Symbol Resin Code 06 PS.svg|class=skin-invert-image|35px]] [[Polystyrene]] (PS)

Beyond the six most widely recognized listed above, there are more commodity plastics that are also mass-produced and commonly used, such as [[polyurethane]]s (PURs). PURs are a class of plastics also designated as commodity plastics due to their low cost, ease of manufacturing, and versatility. However, they lack RICs because they encompass many chemically diverse formulations such as foams and adhesives.

Packaging represents the largest application of commodity plastics, consuming 146 million metric tons (36% of global production) in 2015 alone. Beyond packaging, however, these plastics are critical in various other fields such as agriculture, construction, consumer goods, and healthcare.

Although many traits such as durability and resistance to [[Biodegradation|biodegradability]] are desirable in various applications, they have led to significant environmental issues. An estimated 8 to 12 million tons of plastic enter oceans annually, primarily from mismanaged packaging waste. Commodity plastics account for the majority of this pollution, as their recycling rates remain low (e.g., only ~9% of all plastics are recycled globally). Microplastics derived from their degradation further threaten ecosystems and human health.

The roughly 20% of remaining plastics are engineering and high-performance plastics, valued for their strength, heat resistance, chemical resistance, and other exceptional qualities. These kinds of plastics are more expensive, less common, and often used in more specialized applications.
